item.title: What to Do When There Is Not Enough Testing Time?
item.description:
Product manager: “The client pressure is unbearable, it must go live tomorrow!” Developer: “The code was just merged, no time for thorough self-testing….” Tester: looking at the long list of test cases, can only sigh silently…

Does this scenario feel all too familiar at the sprint stage of every project?

When the project schedule is in jeopardy, development is delayed, requirements change…

All the pressure eventually rolls like a snowball to the last link - testing.

So the test engineer becomes the final “scapegoat” and the “gatekeeper” deciding the project’s fate. And the phrase “not enough testing time” becomes the sword of Damocles hanging over everyone’s head.

But: when testing never has enough time, the problem is by no means only in testing, and the main cause is not even in the testing phase.

Behind this hides a deeper but more common dilemma of team collaboration.

Is “the Testing Phase” Reasonable Just Because It Exists?

In many teams’ workflows, testing is seen as an independent, linear “phase”.

1
2
3
4
5
6

graph LR
A(Requirements) -->B(Design)
 B --> C(Development)
 C -->D[**Testing**]
 D -->E(Release)

The process seems natural, but in actual work it hides great risk.

Once any of the preceding links (such as design or development) has a problem and takes longer than expected, the time left for testing will be ruthlessly compressed. Testing goes from a quality assurance phase to a risk cleanup phase.

QA’s work becomes that of a firefighter, as if forced into a room already full of smoke, trying to find possible sources of fire before the house burns down. Not only inefficient, but extremely dangerous.

Worse, this model also breeds an “us vs. them” adversarial culture:

  • Development thinks: “Why is it all this module after so long testing? Do you even know how to test?”
  • Testing thinks: “What lousy code! So many bugs in one module?”

Everyone no longer seems to be teammates fighting side by side, but stands in opposition to each other.

Obviously, this is not what we want to see!

How to Break the Deadlock?

So how do we break this curse of “not enough time”?

The answer is not the common sight of testers working overtime until dawn, but a fundamental shift in thinking: from “quality assurance” to “quality built in”.

Quality is not “tested” out at the last stage, but “built” throughout the whole process. Testing should not be the final phase of a project either, but a “quality coach” that runs through the whole thing.

**1. Shift Testing Left, Get Involved Early Instead of Waiting for the “Wrap-up”

Do not wait until the code is written to think about testing. Let testers get involved from the very beginning, in requirements review and the design phase.

What are the benefits of early tester involvement?

  • Raise testability questions: Is this requirement’s logic clear? What are the boundary conditions? Are there “black boxes” that are hard to test?
  • Perform risk analysis: Which features are core high-risk areas? Which can have their testing priority appropriately lowered?
  • Prevent defects: Many bugs are already determined at the design stage. QA’s early intervention can “prevent” them at the lowest cost, rather than “finding” them with effort after development is complete.

Turn testers from “problem finders” into “risk preventers” - this is how value is maximized.

2. Embrace Automation to Maximize Tester Value

Manual testing is exploratory and creative, but also time-consuming and error-prone. For regression test cases that are executed repeatedly, test automation is where it shines most.

  • Unit testing: Developers write their own UTs to ensure the stability of code modules.
  • Integration testing: Can ensure collaboration between modules works.
  • End-to-end (E2E) automation: Simulates user operations and covers core business flows.

Integrate test automation into the CI/CD pipeline so it runs automatically on every code commit. This frees testers from heavy regression testing to focus on more valuable exploratory testing and complex scenario testing.

3. Use Good Steel on the Blade

The cruel reality is that we can never have enough time to test 100% of the features. So testing smartly matters more than testing hard.

Together with product and development, define the risk level of each feature based on business impact, usage frequency, and code complexity.

  • High-risk features (such as payment and login): Invest the most time and effort, doing in-depth, comprehensive testing.
  • Medium-risk features: Execute core cases to ensure the main paths are fine.
  • Low-risk features (such as text changes and color adjustments): Verify quickly, or even only verify online.

Apply limited testing resources precisely where they matter most.

4. Quality Is Not Free, It Is Expensive

“This requirement is so simple, why does testing take so long?”

Behind this sentence is an underestimation of the value of testing work.

At the early stage of project planning, all testing-related work - test analysis, test case design, test execution, automation script maintenance, and so on - must be treated as formal tasks and included in project scheduling and effort estimation.

Only when quality is regarded as a “first-class citizen” as important as feature development will it not be easily sacrificed.

5. An “All-Hands Quality” Culture

This is the most important and also the hardest point.

  • Development should be responsible for code quality, writing clear, maintainable code, and completing necessary unit tests.
  • Product should be responsible for requirements quality, providing clear, unambiguous requirements documents.
  • QA should be responsible for the overall quality process, providing professional test strategies and risk feedback.

Only when everyone in the team regards “quality” as their own KPI will there no longer be mutual blame and buck-passing.

Everyone’s goal becomes aligned: to jointly build a product that satisfies users.

Closing Thoughts

“Not enough testing time” has never been an isolated technical problem; it is a process problem, a culture problem, and even more a team collaboration problem.

What we need is not more desperate testing, but a healthier, more efficient collaboration system.

When quality is no longer the endpoint of a phase, but a belief that runs throughout; When QA is no longer a gatekeeper fighting alone, but a quality coach empowering the team!

Only then can the curse of “not enough time” truly be broken.

item.title: Shift-Left Testing Is More Than Testers Getting Involved Early
item.description:
Preface

In the traditional waterfall software development process, testing usually sits late in the SDLC, and testers take on the duty of “quality gatekeeper”. As agile development, DevOps, and other delivery models have been adopted, rapid iteration and continuous delivery have become the norm, and accordingly the concept of “shift-left testing” is mentioned frequently; many agile teams treat “shift-left testing” as an important practice.

Many teams encourage testers to get involved in projects as early as possible, involving testers in requirements, design, and development, including requirements reviews, design discussions, pairing during development, unit/integration testing, continuous integration pipelines, test automation, and so on.

In this article we will not discuss these specific practices of shift-left testing, but rather clarify one point: “shift-left testing” is not merely testers moving toward the front end

Software Quality

What is software quality? The definition in IEEE.1061 is as follows:

Software quality is the degree to which a software product satisfies stated requirements as well as implicit needs arising from user needs and expectations.

This definition is quite abstract, and it also shows indirectly that quality is a product attribute that is rather hard to define precisely.

Roles with different perspectives actually see quality differently.

User Perspective

Quality is the degree to which user needs and expectations are met. That is, can the product help users solve specific problems? Is it convenient and fast? Stable and reliable? Good value for money?

“This software is really easy to use!” “This system is very stable and never crashes!” “This app feels so smooth~”

Developer Perspective

From a developer’s perspective, quality is reflected in the code and architecture.

“Is the code standardized, readable, and maintainable?” “Clear architecture, easy to extend” “Technical debt is under control”

Tester Perspective

From a tester’s perspective, beyond bringing in the user’s experience, quality is more about adaptability across multiple scenarios.

The degree to which the software fits various scenarios such as happy path, angry path, scary path, greedy path, and so on.

Management Perspective

From a management perspective, quality is reflected in whether delivery is on time, whether the budget is under control, and whether product metrics are met.

“The product is delivered on time with high quality” “R&D costs are greatly reduced” “The system runs stably with 99.999% availability”

Business Perspective

From a business operations perspective, quality measures the degree to which the product creates value and competitive advantage.

“User downloads”, “user registrations”, “order conversion rate”, “user retention rate”, and so on….

A thousand Hamlets in a thousand people's eyes - so it is with quality too!

In the end, it comes down to what we often stress: quality is not guaranteed by testing, and testing cannot guarantee it either! Quality is closely tied to the whole team and to everyone in the software lifecycle chain; everyone should be an owner!

The Essence of Shift-Left Testing

With the explanation in the previous section, it becomes easy to understand the point of this article’s title: "shift-left testing" is not merely testers moving forward!

Because of the adoption of rapid iteration and continuous delivery, this quality control measure that emerged accordingly moves testers forward. Although testing-related activities are no longer confined to late-stage verification, if quality still depends on testers’ activities, it is still treating the symptoms rather than the root cause.

Shift-left testing is essentially the popularization of an all-hands quality culture. Testers shifting left should, more importantly, bring the testing mindset - uniquely sensitive to quality risks - to the front end, and drive the whole team to build a quality-first cultural atmosphere.

That is, testing should transform toward [QA]! And the QA here is not Quality Assurance in the traditional sense, which focuses on process control and quality assurance work; it should be a new type of QA suited to the agile model.

Testing’s Transformation Toward QA

Quality Assurance

The traditional QA role, Quality Assurance, is a role dedicated to the quality system and is not the same as the testing role. QA’s work is more about formulating and supervising quality standards, with process control across the entire lifecycle; testing, on the other hand, is more of an engineering role based on testing technology.

With the shift-left trend, testing should no longer be confined to the application of testing technology, but should turn its perspective to Quality Assurance, paying attention to quality risks at every link in the entire software development chain.

Quality Analyzer

That is actually not enough! Shift-left testing is not a role switch; more importantly, it also involves introducing the testing mindset. So at this point, testing should also be a Quality Analyzer. For example:

During requirements review:

Find the gray areas: Proactively identify ambiguities in requirements. For example, “the system response should be fast” - how fast is fast? “A friendly user interface” - how is friendly defined?

Raise “What if” questions: Explore various scenarios, including normal flows, exception flows, and boundary cases:

  • “What happens if the user enters special characters here?”
  • “If the network suddenly drops, how will the data be handled?”
  • “If the user has no permission, what prompt should be shown?”

Ensure requirements are testable: Assess whether each requirement can be verified through concrete operations and expected results

During the architecture/design phase:

Start from the user’s perspective: Check whether the design’s flows are smooth and intuitive

Focus on edge cases: Whether loading states, error prompts, empty-state pages, etc. have all been designed

Assess accessibility: Consider whether the design is friendly to all user groups

Assess system testability: Ensure the system is verifiable, including log recording, traceability of operation flows, third-party mocking, and so on

Assess non-functional requirements and test strategy: Ensure that the architecture and design phase has fully considered performance, security, reliability, and other non-functional requirements, and build corresponding test plans

During development:

Drive unit test coverage: Help the development team build unit test frameworks and improve test coverage

Go deep into system integration: Work with the development team to build a continuous integration CI pipeline based on a suitable branch management model, and build the quality gate for test automation

By deeply participating in the front-end links, test thinking and reflection on and keen observation of software quality are integrated into software development activities beyond testing.

Quality Advocator

In addition, a quality culture does not happen overnight. In a fast-moving team, a role that puts quality first, continuously advocates quality awareness to the team, and can promptly raise “objections” when quality is at risk of losing control is even more an important function of testers after “shift-left testing”.

But for this new function to work, it cannot do without the team’s and management’s consistent recognition of quality first, including institutional support for testers’ related work after shifting left. Otherwise, quality first will mostly remain a formality, nothing more than a catchy slogan.

Conclusion

With the continuous development of agile and DevOps technologies, the speed, rhythm, and complexity of software development keep increasing. In this context, for shift-left testing to be truly implemented, building a quality culture is actually fundamental.

And in this process, testing also needs to complete its role transformation, moving toward quality consultant, quality analyst, and quality advocator, and delivering value on a broader scale.

In short, implementing “shift-left testing” requires integrating quality thinking into every link of development, branding the quality culture into the team’s DNA, and ultimately building a quality ecosystem with full participation and continuous improvement.

item.title: Dare to Be a Dissenter - More on Testers' Perception of Their Role
item.description:
Preface

A few days ago, I read a blog post by the foreign blogger Vitaly Sharovatov, about the “trap of intellectual conformity” in enterprises and R&D teams. Because of the trap of intellectual conformity, many avoidable wrong decisions get pushed through. And testers can play a more critical role in this.

It was quite inspiring to read; after some deep thought, I wrote this article to share with you all~

The Trap of Intellectual Conformity

The trap of intellectual conformity refers to the tendency of an individual who holds a certain position or perception to selectively accept information consistent with it while ignoring or overlooking inconsistent information, thereby forming a self-reinforcing cognitive loop that makes it difficult to assess reality objectively.

In the 1950s, psychologists such as Festinger, Carlsmith, and Solomon Asch conducted many related experiments, confirming the widespread existence of cognitive conformity bias:

  • When performing boring tasks, subjects paid less were more likely than those paid more to change their original evaluation, to rationalize the conflict between their behavior and the outcome.
  • In another experiment, most subjects changed their originally correct choice because of other people’s wrong answers.
  • When the same food was priced differently, subjects tended to believe the more expensive food tasted better.

In short, the experiments above are what we call the “conformity mentality”

Quality Risks Caused by Intellectual Conformity

In enterprises, quality problems caused by the “conformity mentality” above and going along with the majority opinion are not uncommon.

  • A development build that cannot even pass smoke testing is hastily submitted for testing, simply because the developers “feel” it is fine
  • A feature that a leader thought up on a whim is rushed into development, and because it does not meet real user needs, it becomes a white elephant or even has to be rolled back
  • Without investigation of the user base or analysis of real usage scenarios, a new feature is completely unusable

For the problems above, did really no one feel beforehand that something might be wrong? It is just that most people had no opinion, or the process reached a certain node, and it was pushed through by default.

I once saw a view from a startup CEO: software testers are “more harmful than helpful” in terms of cost-effectiveness. If you hire only excellent developers with quality awareness, you do not need a dedicated quality role.

But is that really the case? In my earlier articles, I discussed the difference between “developer thinking” and “tester thinking”:

  • Developers tend to pursue certainty. Based on definite requirements and steps, they define how the product should behave.
  • Testers need to consider various possible paths and branch scenarios based on uncertainty, and assess the product’s possible behavior based on the unknown.

Moreover, in a performance-driven organization, developers are hired to deliver results, not to question. They are evaluated on their ability to build, not on their ability to find and respond to problems.

And based on the trap of intellectual conformity, in an output-oriented organization, dissenting voices are continuously weakened, so even developers with excellent quality awareness find it hard to put quality first in such an environment.

Testing, the “Dissenter” Assigned by the Role

Many people with a “conformity mentality” can actually sense that something is wrong; they just lack the courage to raise a “dissent”. But once a challenger appears who points out the problem, they too can actively offer opinions.

And the testing role, by its very design, is assigned and expected to raise questions and challenges.

This is precisely the necessity for the testing role to exist and matter: lowering the threshold for others to dissent and creating space for critical thinking in the team.

As testers, we should not confine ourselves to the limits of the development lifecycle; we should actively shift testing left and participate more in earlier phases, so as to better demonstrate the value of the role.

Of course, recognizing this also means accepting the positioning of being the “bearer of bad news”. Face it calmly; a team’s path to success cannot do without such a role.

Conclusion

Those who enjoy watching historical costume dramas should be familiar that in every dynasty there was an office such as the “censor” or “remonstrance official”. As advisers who spoke truth to power, they were mostly unwelcome to emperors and ministers, yet the operation of the system could not do without this function of supervision and review.

And testers are very much like the “censors” in the system of software development.

Do not fear the “fail” on a test report; that is precisely the meaning of the testing function’s existence.

item.title: Fourteen Years Later, Revisiting "Testing Is Dead"
item.description:
Introduction

Going back fourteen years, to October 2011, at Google’s GTAC (Google Test Automation Conference), Alberto Savoia walked onto the stage dressed as the Grim Reaper and dramatically declared that “software testing is dead”.

Soon after, the testing heavyweight Jame Whittaker made the same declaration, Test is Dead, at another testing conference, EuroSTAR.

The point of these remarks was the belief that software testing no longer needs to be an independent role in the software development process. With mature software processes and tools, macro-level quality problems no longer require a relatively large, dedicated team to guarantee them. Instead, testing should evolve into a series of micro-activities distributed among other roles, such as project managers, developers, and even end users. Distribute testing activities across other phases of development.

And as this manifesto spread widely, many tech giants, including Google and Microsoft, began to cut dedicated testing positions, and testing transformed into test development or software efficiency departments.

But more than a decade later, has the testing profession really died out? On the contrary, Whittaker himself published an article last year (2024) titled “The Resurrection of Software Testing”, re-examining the evolution of the testing industry (original text at https://medium.com/@docjamesw/the-resurrection-of-software-testing-634423cd8411)

In this article, let’s delve into this topic again.

The Recurring Claim That “Testing Is Dead”

From the time the “testing is dead” claim was made, it has in fact been raised many times. This saying has recurred in at least three periods:

  1. The Selenium open-source era: As automated testing tools gradually entered everyday enterprise use, machines replacing humans seemed within reach
  2. The era of rampant automation frameworks and platforms: A large number of automated testing solutions flooded the market, all claiming they could greatly reduce testing work
  3. Today’s AI era: With AI now in full swing, the old tune is replayed, claiming AI can already replace the work of testers

Why?

Actually, on careful reflection, this cyclical recurrence is no accident; it reflects a common misalignment between technological change and industry perception. Whenever a new technology appears, people tend to be overly optimistic that it can completely replace human judgment and creativity.

Beyond that, the testing industry’s own perception of testing largely supplies fuel for this claim.

Many training institutions, and many testers themselves, do not regard testing as a discipline

  • Enter the field with zero background
  • Even a novice can do testing
  • Testing is nothing but “clicking around”
  • Knowing how to write automation scripts makes you a senior tester

Companies confuse automation with testing

Many companies vigorously promote automation and set up test-development positions.

But they fail to truly recognize that so-called automated testing is, more often than not, just checking, which is far from real testing.

Test developers spend a great deal of time building frameworks and platforms, trying every means to improve efficiency with tools, but there are few real cases of achievements in expanding testing thinking or digging out deep quality problems.

Unclear testing goals

As said before, there are many who believe testing exists to verify requirements. Testers are more like “quality inspectors” holding a checklist, judging by whether specifications are met rather than whether the product can deliver value.

It is precisely these widespread misconceptions across the testing industry that do enormous harm to testing itself.

But even after testing positions are cut? TDD, BDD, and starting with the end in mind mean developers actually take on testing duties; or end customers are made to act as testers without knowing it, and once they find a problem, people scramble to fix it quickly.

So it is not that testing is dead; only the party responsible for performing testing and the division of responsibilities have shifted.

What Kind of “Testing” Should Truly Die Out?

Just as I have stressed in several earlier articles about the real purpose of software testing. 【】

The true purpose of testing is neither simply to verify requirements nor merely to find bugs.

A clear distinction should also be drawn between testing and checking. As technology advances, the checking part of testing is what should gradually be weakened and removed from testing responsibilities.

Automated testing, those checklists of test cases and the green progress bars on CI dashboards, really cannot count as testing genuinely oriented toward quality; all they bring is a false sense of security.

These “checkbox activities” that tick through items according to pre-written scripts are the part that should truly be distinguished from testing and should die out.

Spending large amounts of time writing and maintaining these formalized test cases and test scripts actually reduces the real testing time available for exploring the product and gaining insight into risks, and in fact harms the true value of testing.

Automated Testing vs. Real Testing

We must clarify the following core understanding:

Automated testing is usually only used to check what is already known, the behavior we expect the system to perform. Real testing, on the other hand, is about the unknown. It is a discipline that requires investigation, exploration, questioning, reasoning, experimentation, and verification. No script or AI can fully replace it.

The true value of testing should always lie in exploring the unknown, in discovering problems that cannot be foreseen through automation.

Redefining the Value of Testing

Testing is not only about finding bugs, nor only about tools. Its value should include:

  • Understanding product risks: Identifying potential problems that could affect users or the business
  • Communicating uncertainty: Clearly conveying findings about product quality and risk
  • Modeling user behavior: Predicting how real users will interact with the system
  • Finding problems others missed: Offering a unique perspective and insight

These values are indispensable in any software development lifecycle. When an organization truly understands these values, testing will inevitably take an important role in the software development process, whether performed by dedicated testers or by developers and other roles.

Conclusion

Testing has never died; it only keeps being reborn!

The “testing is dead” claim surfaces every few years, but testing has never truly died. It only keeps evolving - from manual testing to automation, from an independent role to distributed responsibility, from verifying the known to exploring the unknown. Every evolution is the result of testing adapting to new environments and new technologies.

Today, as we face the wave of AI, the same story is replaying. Some predict AI will replace testers, but history tells us that technology changes the way testing is done, not the need for it. AI can automate more tasks, but the critical thinking, creativity, and systems thinking of human testers remain irreplaceable.

The future of testing does not lie in resisting change, but in embracing evolution. Testers need to develop new skills and adopt new tools, but more importantly, they must hold fast to the core value of testing - exploring the unknown, assessing risk, and safeguarding quality.

item.title: When AI Writes Applications, a Blessing or a Challenge for Quality?
item.description:
When AI Writes Applications, a Blessing or a Challenge for Quality?

As AI models become increasingly capable, AI programming tools represented by Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, and Gemini Cli are gradually entering everyday software development, and “vibe coding” is increasingly becoming a trend in application development.

So when AI becomes more and more involved in the development of real applications, is the quality of applications built in this way good or bad?

This article shares my views based on my recent experience using several vibe coding tools.

AI Programming Looks Beautiful

From the moment people first encounter AI programming, many are amazed by its extremely fast and efficient power. Combined with good prompt engineering, it can often complete prototype design in a very short time, and the resulting product is frequently more feature-complete than expected.

As long as we have some understanding of software application development, combined with prompt engineering, AI can help us with everything from design to code, from the front end and back end to the database. What engineers need to do seems to be continuously communicating with the AI and constantly optimizing and adjusting the output.

It can be said that the emergence of AI programming tools has enabled many non-programmers to develop a wide range of creative applications, greatly lowering the barrier to software development.

In major software development companies, it is gradually becoming the norm for developers to write more and more code with the help of AI tools.

The future of AI programming is so close, and so beautiful~

However, if the goal is not merely to validate a prototype, and we judge an AI-developed application by the standards of a production-grade application, then a complex and painful debugging process will inevitably be part of the picture.

“Ten minutes of development, two whole days of debugging” is actually the norm when it comes to AI programming.

When the AI’s Imagination Leaves You Speechless

Although “prompt engineering” summarizes and emphasizes some of the best ways to collaborate with AI, in real work, engineers often still tend to communicate with the AI using brief instructions.

When such instructions are insufficient and imprecise, the AI will naturally imagine a great deal of code that it considers necessary but that is actually plausible yet wrong. At this point, engineers inevitably need to spend a large amount of time checking and adjusting the AI’s behavior.

Anyone who has coded with AI has likely had the experience of spending a huge amount of time on some basic logic or front-end interface adjustment.

For example, I once encountered a case where I simply wanted to add a field to a page form and adjust the back-end database accordingly. Yet the AI always misread the intent — either it didn’t sync the change, or it modified other unrelated forms. The back-and-forth dragged on and consumed a lot of time.

What should have been a two-line change turned into a situation where, because I wasn’t familiar with the structure of the AI-generated code, I relied on the AI to revise it over and over. Although the desired result was finally achieved, a large amount of needless spaghetti code was inserted along the way.

Weaknesses in Integration and Decoupling

When AI generates code, it generally first determines the project’s code structure based on the initial requirements, and then fills in the code according to specific decomposed tasks.

But as the project progresses and requirements are continuously refined, the main logic usually ends up concentrated in a few main files, which easily makes some of those files overly bloated. And because AI relies on large models, which usually have context window limitations, bloated files greatly constrain the efficiency and quality of code generation.

Therefore, as requirements are continuously detailed and adjusted, the code becomes increasingly bloated and increasingly chaotic. It rarely undergoes proper decoupling and refactoring as it would in real engineering practice, and the AI’s own understanding of the code often becomes more and more difficult, making it hard to recapture that initial sense of amazement.

At this point, engineer intervention is essential; otherwise, AI coding becomes more like trying to carve flowers on a dunghill.

What You See Is Not Necessarily What You Get

In order to present results quickly, AI-generated code sometimes “cheats” by hard-coding the presentation of certain data effects.

In the early stage, some mock data may be indispensable to demonstrate results. But you cannot fully trust the AI to distinguish hard-coding from properly handled logic.

In an AI-assisted tool I once used, I pointed out to it that after I entered a certain specific piece of data, the actual result didn’t match expectations. After pretending to analyze things for a long time, the AI told me it had found the cause. But when I actually checked the code, I discovered that its handling of this part was simply an if check targeting that specific piece of data, forcing a special case and calling it a day.

Challenges to Quality

So, from the explanations (and complaints) above, although AI has achieved astonishing results in assisting coding, and there is no lack of cases where it cooperates well with engineers, many applications generated with AI assistance still cannot dispel concerns about questionable quality.

Perhaps AI itself can help you generate unit tests, but just as intelligent driving still cannot replace human decision-making, in the field of quality, the role of human test engineers remains irreplaceable. Indeed, as AI applications become more widespread, the importance of manual testing becomes ever more prominent.

  • The quality of the code itself
  • Overall planning of complex applications and broad-context understanding
  • Deficiencies in scalability, performance, security, and other aspects
  • Mock data and hard-coding

How Test Engineers Should Respond

Given the quality challenges of AI-generated applications, test engineers should also carry out targeted testing and verification of their output.

The following aspects can be considered as priorities:

Systematic Verification Against Traditional Standards

As a product, testing should first and foremost verify the finished AI application from the perspectives of requirements, product goals, and user usage, ensuring that it meets product requirements and quality standards.

Product Integration, Scalability, Performance, and Security

In view of the weak points of AI code, focus on scenarios such as product integration, scalability, performance, and security, and carry out targeted testing.

From Black Box to White Box

The existence of AI illusions requires test engineers not only to verify the application from a black-box perspective, but also to pay attention to the process by which the AI generated the application. In particular, during the development process, the relevant prompts, context, and records of the AI’s responses are all sources for understanding potential quality problems. Many issues, such as hard-coding, may be hidden in some misleading interactions.

Embrace AI and Fight Magic with Magic

Although AI still has many problems, and using it incorrectly can produce products of poor quality, using it properly can indeed provide great help.

With AI, we can analyze product code and sort out the project architecture, helping us better understand the implementation of the project. This includes using AI to assist with many testing tasks, including automated testing.

Conclusion

All in all, a good-quality product cannot do without a mature team and standardized processes. For testers, the AI era is also an opportunity to redefine our role. Embracing the challenges of AI-driven development, testers will also be indispensable participants and collaborators. Embrace AI, and embrace the future!

item.title: Is Testing Really Inferior to Development?
item.description:
Someone asked whether people who do testing are really inferior to developers?

Although everyone has their own view, it is still worth thinking about the mainstream view represented behind this question.

Below I share Qiucao’s perspective.

Testing Technology and Development Technology Are Not the Same Track

First of all, to truly do the testing job well, the skill requirements are actually quite high. But testing technology and development technology are technologies of different dimensions. A developer complaining about testers by comparing software development skills is like a basketball player mocking a swimmer for being slow at running.

Testing technology includes many requirements that differ from development technology; for details, see my other earlier article 【】, which I will not repeat here.

Real Reasons Why Testing Is Underrated

But we must also recognize this objective fact — in most enterprises, the say, salary, and so on of the testing position are usually a notch lower than those of developers at the same level.

There are in fact multiple reasons for this situation, mainly the general perception of the role and a rather harsh industry environment. Specifically:

The Mismatch Between Job Requirements and Expected Output

First of all, most current testing job requirements actually revolve around verifying requirements — including test case design and test automation implementation, all of which are based on the verification of existing requirements.

But verifying requirements is actually more checking work than testing work.

Checking, as a subset of testing, actually has lower requirements and does not demand much technical skill. Correspondingly, job requirements centered on requirement verification are in fact requirements for a low-skill position.

The contradiction, however, is that the expectation of the testing position is to guarantee comprehensive quality after the product is released. And the coverage requirements for product quality simply cannot be achieved through requirement verification alone.

Requirement verification is mainly about functional coverage, and usually includes only basic scenarios, lacking all kinds of abnormal scenarios and non-functional scenarios. To achieve quality coverage, it is necessary to rely on full-process quality control during the development phase, including the testing work in the testing phase. Here, testing is not merely basic checking — it must also include proactive discovery supported by a wider range of testing techniques.

And this mismatch between job requirements and expected output also leads to doubts about the effectiveness of the testing position.

Lower Job Requirements Lead to a Lower Industry Barrier

When the job requirements themselves mainly target low-skill checking work, the entry barrier to the industry is naturally lowered too, and many newcomers with little experience or skill can enter the industry to perform the relevant checking work.

In earlier years there was even a distinction between test design engineers and test execution engineers; here, test execution merely required following the cases to carry out operations and record the results. Such the most basic checking work can hardly be said to require much testing technology.

A relatively low level of skill and job requirements naturally affects the overall evaluation of the position.

The Industry’s Own Misdirection

The rapid development of the IT industry in earlier years and its relatively good compensation made IT a popular career choice. And for the reasons mentioned above, when low-skill checking work is dressed up in the clothes of testing work, such testing positions become the best entry channel for non-IT people to get into the industry.

A large number of non-IT professionals hoping to enter the industry in turn generated a great deal of demand for training.

Then, fueled by all kinds of training institutions — including hype about entering the industry with zero background and newcomers earning high salaries — large numbers of people were indeed delivered into the industry. The performance at work of these short-term, fast-track “talents” naturally affected the overall evaluation of the industry.

The Hardest-Hit Area in the Industry Winter

As the IT winter arrived, enterprises, under cost pressure, cut spending and reduced headcount. Combined with all the factors mentioned above, this made testing the hardest-hit area — a vicious cycle in which the common perception of the testing position drifted even further from the value it deserves.

In Closing

Objectively speaking, it is true that a large number of practitioners in the so-called “testing industry” in China today can hardly be called qualified, so saying it is inferior to development positions is not entirely wrong.

But the “testing” here is in quotation marks — checking and testing are being confused as one.

All in all, the overall environment of the entire testing industry today is rather harsh and misunderstandings run deep, and Qiucao feels quite powerless about it.

There is no need to lose heart, however. If you build your own capability around the true goals of the role and deliver genuine value for comprehensive quality, you will naturally be the one still standing when the tide recedes.

item.title: Testability Is More Than Just Code
item.description:
In the field of software development, we often define testability (Testability) as a technical metric: whether the code is easy to test.

In this article, let’s discuss it from a different perspective: testability is not only about code, but also about human nature.

Testability from a Traditional Perspective

In most technical discussions, testability is confined to a narrow scope. We talk about modularity, dependency injection, logging, and interface design — all of these are meant to make the code easier to be covered by automated scripts or unit tests.

Such a focus is understandable, because a well-designed system can indeed lower testing costs.

However, stopping here means seeing only the tip of the iceberg.

The success of a software product ultimately depends on whether it can run stably in the real world, and that real world is full of complex human factors and environmental challenges.

If our testability only focuses on whether the code is easy to test, then we ignore the most critical question:

For a specific person, in a specific situation, to test a specific product — exactly how easy is it?

True Testability

Test engineers should be familiar with the following scenarios:

  • Automation test engineers spend most of a day not writing scripts, but dealing with unstable test environments. Network fluctuations, service outages, and data pollution — factors unrelated to the code itself — can bring testing to a complete standstill. By the time the environment is finally ready, a whole day’s energy has often been exhausted.

  • Test teams need to go through complex configuration and dependency installation steps before they can start certain tests, which makes manual testing and exploratory testing extremely inefficient. Under time pressure, team members may have to give up some tests, or can only perform the most superficial functional verification.

  • There is a lack of smooth communication between developers and testers. When a feature is hard to test because of high code coupling, testers often find themselves in a difficult position, while developers have a hard time realizing the difficulty this creates during testing and fail to provide timely assistance.

All of the problems above, without exception, point to one fact:

True testability often does not lie in the complexity of the code, but in the entire ecosystem built around the product, and the people within it.

A product that is hard to test brings more than just release delays. It also drains the team’s energy and stifles testers’ curiosity and desire to explore.

Moreover, it can even create a false sense of security that “the product is stable.” When defects that should have been found are missed because testing is too difficult, it is the quality after release and the end users that are ultimately affected.

How to Improve Testability

Once we understand the human dimension of testability, how should we solve this problem?

Actually, the focus is a shift from “making code easier to test” to “making testers more able to test.”

1. Redefining “Easy to Test”

When defining product features, consider more comprehensively:

  • Tool support: Do testers have handy tools?
  • Team culture: Does the team encourage sharing testing pain points and solving them together?
  • Business knowledge: Do testers fully understand the business requirements?
  • Work environment: Is the test environment stable and reliable?

2. Minimizing Obstacles

In a fast-paced iteration cycle, we always think “speed” is the top priority. But it should be noted that the real bottleneck is not speed, but all kinds of obstacles. Reducing the friction in the testing process is more valuable than simply increasing test execution speed. This includes:

  • Simplifying environment setup: Use containerization technologies (such as Docker) or automation scripts to make test environment deployment a one-click process.
  • Clear documentation: Provide clear architecture diagrams, API documentation, and testing guides for complex systems, so newcomers can get started quickly.
  • Toolchain integration: Ensure that testing tools, CI/CD pipelines, and reporting systems work together seamlessly.

3. Tracking the Degree of Testability with Reasonable Metrics

We can reflect the degree of testability in testing by collecting and tracking some testing process data.

  • Environment readiness time: On average, how long does it take to prepare a usable test environment?
  • Defect reproduction cost: How many steps and how much time does it take to reproduce a defect found in a production environment?
  • Feature testing time: How long does it take for a feature to go from development completion to passing testing?

These metrics help us measure testability more directly and help us make targeted improvements.

Conclusion

Testability is, in essence, a topic about empathy and humanism.

We should shift from the perspective of product attributes, to the perspective of supporting testers, and then expand to the perspective of collaboration across the entire team.

Technology serves people, and the ultimate guarantee of software quality comes from respect for and support of people.

item.title: The Two Sides of Applying Docker in Test Automation
item.description:
Preface

Test automation is an indispensable part of software development today. To ensure consistency of the test environment, simplify configuration, and speed up test feedback, Docker technology is widely applied in test automation frameworks for containerized packaging.

The common consensus is that once a test suite is Dockerized, it achieves the ideal state of “build once, run anywhere”, completely eliminating the test uncertainty caused by environmental differences.

In real engineering practice, however, can Dockerization truly guarantee perfect consistency of test execution? In this article we will take a deeper look at the promises and the reality of Docker in test automation, uncover the key factors that can lead to the “illusion of consistency”, and offer corresponding mitigation strategies.

Docker’s Promise - Environment Packaging and Consistency

Docker’s core value lies in using an image to package the complete runtime environment of an application (the operating system layer, runtime, libraries, tools, code, and configuration). Its workflow is typically as follows:

  1. Build the image: In a development environment (such as a developer’s local PC), define dependency installation and configuration steps through a Dockerfile, and build an image containing the test suite and its runtime environment.
  2. Distribute the image: Push the built image to an image registry (such as Docker Hub or Artifactory).
  3. Run the container: In the target environment (a CI/CD pipeline, another developer’s machine, a pre-production environment, etc.), pull the image and instantiate it as a container to execute the tests.

In theory, this flow should ensure that regardless of the specific configuration of the underlying host, the test execution environment inside the container always stays consistent, thereby eliminating the classic developer problem of “it works on my machine” and achieving reliable reproduction of test results.

The Reality - An Illusion of Consistency

Ideals are rich, reality is lean. Although Docker provides powerful environment isolation, the following factors can still break the absolute consistency of tests and create an “illusion”:

Cross-Platform Host Architecture Differences

An image built on an x86 host, when run on an ARM-based CI node (such as Apple Silicon M1/M2), can cause binaries that depend on specific CPU instruction sets, or Python packages containing C extensions, to malfunction or crash, so that tests passing locally fail in CI.

Reason: Docker containers share the host’s kernel. The instruction sets of different CPU architectures (x86_64 vs arm64) are incompatible.

How to Solve It?

  • Multi-architecture image builds: Use the docker buildx tool to build images that support multiple platforms (such as linux/amd64, linux/arm64).
  • Explicitly specify the platform: When running or building, force the target platform via the --platform parameter (e.g., docker run --platform linux/amd64 my-test-image).

External Dependencies

The test container may run perfectly well, but if a test case needs to access real services outside the container (a database, an API, S3, or internal systems reachable only via VPN), then test results can fluctuate due to the status of those external services, network latency, DNS resolution differences, firewall rules, or VPN connection state.

Reason: What Docker containerizes is the test suite itself, not all the external systems it depends on. Network requests break through the container’s isolation boundary.

How to Solve It?

  • Containerize dependencies: Use Docker Compose to dynamically spin up the required external services (such as a database or a Mock server) as separate containers at test runtime, and establish an internal network connection with the test container.
  • Mock/Stub techniques: Widely apply Mock and Stub techniques in unit and integration tests to replace real external dependency calls.
  • Network environment control: Strictly manage the test environment’s network configuration (DNS, proxies, firewalls) to ensure predictability.

Host Operating System Differences

Volume mount operations or network access (localhost) that work fine on a Linux host can, on macOS or Windows (via Docker Desktop), produce file permission errors, broken symbolic links, line-ending (CRLF vs LF) issues, failed inotify event watching, or ambiguity in what localhost points to.

Reason: Although the OS inside the container is consistent, the mechanisms by which Docker interacts with the host OS differ:

  • File volume mounts: These involve mapping the host file system to the container file system, and different OSes support file permissions, metadata, and event notifications differently.
  • Network model: On Linux, container networking is usually more directly integrated; on macOS/Windows, Docker Desktop uses a VM bridge, and accessing host services requires the special hostname host.docker.internal instead of localhost.

How to Solve It?

  • Understand platform differences: Be clearly aware that Docker is not entirely OS-agnostic and that its behavior is influenced by the host.
  • Use volume mounts cautiously: Avoid having core test logic depend heavily on host volume mounts, especially for write operations (such as generating reports or caches). Prefer in-container paths or the copy (COPY) mechanism. If a mount is necessary, pay attention to file permissions and line-ending issues.
  • Use the correct network access method: When accessing host services from inside a container, consistently use host.docker.internal (Mac/Windows) or understand the service access rules under Docker network modes (bridge/host) (Compose service names). Avoid hardcoding localhost.

Resource Constraints

Tests pass on a well-resourced local development machine (say, 16 cores and 32GB RAM), but when run on a resource-constrained CI node (where the CPU may be throttled, memory may be insufficient, or resources are shared with other tasks), tests fail or become flaky due to timeouts and resource contention (CPU, IO).

Reason: Docker containers share the host’s physical resources (CPU, memory, disk IO, network bandwidth). CI environments usually have lower resource quotas than development machines and are subject to contention.

How to Solve It?

  • Resource limits and monitoring: Set explicit resource limits (--cpus, --memory) for the test container in the Docker run command or Compose file to bring it closer to the CI environment. Monitor resource usage on the CI node.
  • Performance optimization: Optimize test cases and the framework itself to reduce resource consumption (e.g., controlling parallelism, avoiding memory leaks, optimizing I/O operations).
  • Choose a matching CI environment: Ensure the CI environment’s baseline resource configuration meets the minimum requirements for running the tests.

Mutable Dependencies and Version Drift - The Hidden Risk of the “latest” Tag

During image builds, using a base image tag like FROM python:latest, or not strictly locking dependency versions with pip install -r requirements.txt (without using pip freeze or a lock file), can cause later builds to introduce incompatibilities or bugs due to unexpected upgrades of underlying dependencies (the Python interpreter, libraries), undermining test stability.

Reason: A dependency’s “latest” tag or an unlocked version number will point to a new version over time, introducing uncertainty.

How to Solve It?

  • Strict version locking: In the Dockerfile, use a base image tag with a definite version (such as FROM python:3.11-slim). Use a lock file (such as requirements.txt with an explicit version for each dependency, or poetry.lock/Pipfile.lock) to manage dependencies.
  • Reproducible builds: Ensure that every build, based on the same lock file, produces a completely identical image. Periodically and deliberately update dependency versions and re-test to verify.

A Rational View of Docker’s Value and Engineering Practice

Despite all the problems above, we still should not deny the tremendous value of Docker in test automation. In environment standardization, simplifying dependency management, and making CI/CD pipelines easier to manage, it still has irreplaceable advantages.

So when applying Docker, the key is to understand: Docker is a powerful tool for achieving consistency, but it is not a one-and-for-all “silver bullet”. Technology only delivers its value through sound engineering practices and effective constraints!

Summary

Docker has built a sturdy “fence” around the consistency of test automation environments, greatly improving the credibility and efficiency of testing. Yet that “fence” is not airtight.

Host architecture differences, the intrusion of external dependencies, OS interaction characteristics, resource contention, and dependency version drift can all quietly erode the expected absolute consistency.

Achieving truly reliable Dockerized test automation requires not only skillful use of Docker itself, but also rigorous engineering practice - defining environment boundaries, strict dependency management, optimized resource usage, and continuous monitoring and improvement. Only in this way can we effectively dispel the “illusion of consistency” and let Docker truly become a solid cornerstone for software quality.

So the next time we hear “No problem, it has already been containerized with Docker”, it is worth asking a few more questions:

  • What architecture does it run on?
  • Are the dependencies locked?
  • How are network and file access handled?
  • Are the resources sufficient?

Know yourself and know your enemy, and you can plan with confidence.

Preface

In the field of test automation, the hottest automation framework today is undoubtedly Playwright. When it comes to page element location — extremely critical in test automation — compared with traditional tools such as Selenium, it introduces a new element-location method, getByRole, which fully leverages the ARIA Roles objects defined by the W3C to identify elements. While improving the flexibility and efficiency of element identification, it simultaneously verifies the accessibility compliance of the page. For example:

await page.getByRole('button', { name: '搜索' }).click();

// Locate the checkbox and check it
await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: '同意条款' }).check();

// Locate the text input and fill in content
await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: '用户名' }).fill('testuser');

// Locate the dropdown and select an option
await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: '国家' }).selectOption('中国');

Today, AI is increasingly taking part in our daily work. As shown in the earlier 【】 article, driving a page through an mcp server to complete automated testing with AI has become quite feasible in practice. After that article, many readers remained skeptical about how AI actually recognizes and locates page elements, drives execution through tools, and whether the results in real use can meet expectations.

In fact, the ARIA standard within the W3C web specifications plays an important role here: it presents page objects to AI in a structured form, making it easier for AI to analyze the page. In this article, we will explore the ARIA standard and its important role in AI-driven test automation.

What is ARIA?

Definition

WAI-ARIA (Web Accessibility Initiative – Accessible Rich Internet Applications), i.e. the Web Accessibility Initiative – Accessible Rich Internet Applications standard, is a specification that enables web applications to better support use by people with disabilities.

ARIA Roles are a set of attributes defined in the W3C WAI-ARIA specification, used to describe the function and purpose of web elements and to help assistive technologies (such as screen readers) understand and convey page content more accurately. **ARIA Roles ** are added to HTML elements through the role attribute; for example, <div role="button"> indicates that the div element should be treated as a button.

Evolution of the Standard and the Advantages of ARIA

This standard has gone through three important stages of development:

  • 2008: W3C first released ARIA 1.0
  • 2014: ARIA 1.1 introduced new roles such as searchbox, switch
  • 2021: ARIA 1.2 added comment, mark, and other roles related to digital content

Comparison with traditional UI test automation:

Dimension Traditional UI Testing ARIA-Based Testing
Element Identification Basis DOM Structure / Visual Features Semantic Roles / Functional Attributes
Maintenance Cost High (frequent updates as UI changes) Low (role definitions are more stable)
Cross-Platform Consistency Depends on the rendering engine Standardized behavior
Accessibility Support Requires additional verification Built-in support

Categories of ARIA Roles

According to the W3C specification, ARIA Roles can be divided into the following major categories:

  1. Widget Roles: describe interactive UI components

    • button: a clickable button
    • checkbox: a checkbox
    • radio: a radio button
    • textbox: a text input box
    • combobox: a dropdown combo box
    • slider: a slider control

  2. Document Structure Roles: describe the structure of page content

    • heading: a heading (alternative to h1-h6)
    • list/listitem: a list and list items
    • table/row/cell: table structure
    • img: an image

  3. Landmark Roles: identify the main regions of a page

    • banner: page header
    • navigation: navigation region
    • main: main content
    • search: search region
    • contentinfo: footer information

  4. Live Region Roles: regions for dynamic content updates

    • alert: important information that needs immediate notification
    • status: feedback on operation status
    • timer: a timer or counter

In addition to the basic Roles, advanced roles commonly used in modern web applications also include:

  • Composite component roles:

 </div>

The Core Role of ARIA in AI-Driven Testing

Enhanced Semantic Understanding

An AI test system, through the semantic network built by ARIA roles, can understand UI functions more accurately:

Intelligent Test Case Generation

W3C ARIA Roles and Their Application in Playwright Test Automation

As a test automation engineer, understanding and correctly applying ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) Roles from the W3C standard is essential for building accessible web applications and writing reliable automated test scripts. This article introduces the core concepts, categories, and best practices of ARIA Roles in detail, with a focus on how to effectively leverage these roles for element location and verification within the Playwright testing framework.

I. Overview of ARIA Roles

1.1 What Are ARIA Roles

ARIA Roles are a set of attributes defined in the W3C WAI-ARIA specification, used to describe the function and purpose of web elements and to help assistive technologies (such as screen readers) understand and convey page content more accurately. ARIA Roles are added to HTML elements through the role attribute; for example, <div role="button"> indicates that the div element should be treated as a button.

1.2 The Importance of ARIA Roles

In web test automation, ARIA Roles offer the following advantages:

  1. Enhanced element semantics: provide clear semantics for custom controls or non-standard HTML elements
  2. Improved test reliability: compared with fragile CSS selectors or XPath, role-based location is more stable
  3. Accessibility testing support: verify whether the application complies with accessibility standards (WCAG)
  4. Cross-browser consistency: ARIA Roles behave consistently across different browsers, reducing test discrepancies

II. Categories of ARIA Roles and Common Roles

2.1 Main Categories of ARIA Roles

According to the W3C specification, ARIA Roles can be divided into the following major categories:

  1. Widget Roles: describe interactive UI components

    • button: a clickable button
    • checkbox: a checkbox
    • radio: a radio button
    • textbox: a text input box
    • combobox: a dropdown combo box
    • slider: a slider control

  2. Document Structure Roles: describe the structure of page content

    • heading: a heading (alternative to h1-h6)
    • list/listitem: a list and list items
    • table/row/cell: table structure
    • img: an image

  3. Landmark Roles: identify the main regions of a page

    • banner: page header
    • navigation: navigation region
    • main: main content
    • search: search region
    • contentinfo: footer information

  4. Live Region Roles: regions for dynamic content updates

    • alert: important information that needs immediate notification
    • status: feedback on operation status
    • timer: a timer or counter

2.2 Examples of Common ARIA Roles

<!-- Button role -->
<div role="button" tabindex="0" aria-pressed="false">Custom button</div>

<!-- Navigation region -->
<nav role="navigation">

 <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
 </ul>
</nav>

<!-- Alert message -->
<div role="alert" aria-live="assertive">

<!-- Progress bar -->
<div role="progressbar" aria-valuenow="75" aria-valuemin="0" aria-valuemax="100"></div>

III. ARIA in Playwright

3.1 Element Location Based on ARIA Roles

Playwright provides a dedicated getByRole() locator method, which is the best way to locate elements using ARIA Roles. Compared with traditional CSS or XPath selectors, role-based location is more stable and semantically explicit.

Basic syntax:

1

await page.getByRole('button', { name: '提交' }).click();

Common role location examples:

// Locate the checkbox and check it
await page.getByRole('checkbox', { name: '同意条款' }).check();

// Locate the text input and fill in content
await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: '用户名' }).fill('testuser');

// Locate the dropdown and select an option
await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: '国家' }).selectOption('中国');

3.2 Option Parameters of the Role Locator

The getByRole() method supports a variety of option parameters for more precise element location:

 expanded: true, // whether expanded (for menus, etc.)
 disabled: false, // whether disabled
 checked: false, // whether checked (checkbox/radio button)
 selected: false, // whether selected (tabs, etc.)
 includeHidden: false, // whether to include hidden elements
 exact: true // whether the name matches exactly
});

3.3 Verifying ARIA Attributes and States

Playwright can not only locate elements but also verify ARIA attributes and states:

// Verify whether the button is disabled

// Verify whether the checkbox is checked

// Verify whether the element is visible
await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toBeVisible();

// Verify the element's ARIA attribute value
const button = page.getByRole('button', { name: '展开' });
await expect(button).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');

IV. ARIA Snapshot Testing in Playwright

Playwright provides a powerful ARIA snapshot feature that can capture and verify the accessibility tree structure of a page.

4.1 ARIA Snapshot Basics

An ARIA snapshot is a YAML representation of the page’s accessibility tree, containing the roles, names, states, and hierarchical relationships of elements:

1
2
3
4
5

- banner:
 - heading "欢迎页面" [level=1]
- main:
 - button "提交"
 - textbox "用户名" [placeholder="请输入用户名"]

4.2 Snapshot Matching Assertions

Use toMatchAriaSnapshot() for snapshot verification:

1
2
3
4

await expect(page.locator('body')).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
 - heading "欢迎页面" [level=1]
 - button "提交"
`);

4.3 Partial Matching and Regular Expressions

Snapshots support flexible partial matching:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

// Match the role only, not the name
await expect(page.locator('dialog')).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
 - dialog
`);

// Use a regular expression to match dynamic text
await expect(page.locator('body')).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
 - heading /订单 \d+/
`);

4.4 Generating and Updating Snapshots 

1
2

# Update snapshots using the --update-snapshots flag
npx playwright test --update-snapshots

Or generate it programmatically:

1
2

const snapshot = await page.locator('#main').ariaSnapshot();
console.log(snapshot);

V. Best Practices for ARIA Testing

5.1 Principles for Using Roles

  1. Prefer native HTML elements: e.g., use <button> instead of <div role="button">
  2. Avoid redundant roles: e.g., <nav role="navigation"> is redundant because <nav> already implies that role
  3. Combine roles and attributes correctly: e.g., role="checkbox" should be used together with aria-checked

5.2 Playwright Testing Recommendations

  1. Prefer ARIA locators: more stable and reliable than CSS/XPath
  2. Combine with accessible names: use the name option to improve location accuracy
  3. Verify dynamic ARIA states: such as aria-expanded, aria-selected, etc.
  4. Check ARIA snapshots regularly: ensure the page structure complies with accessibility standards
  5. Test keyboard navigation: use page.keyboard to test accessibility

5.3 Common Issue Troubleshooting

  1. Element not visible: add includeHidden: true or check the aria-hidden attribute
  2. Name mismatch: use exact: false or a regular expression
  3. Dynamic content: use await expect().toHaveAttribute() to wait for state changes
  4. Custom controls: ensure appropriate ARIA roles and attributes are added

VI. ARIA in Complex Components

6.1 Navigation Menu Testing

 - menuitem "首页"
 - menuitem "产品"

await page.getByRole('tab', { name: '高级设置' }).click();

 - heading "确认删除" [level=2]
 - button "取消"
 - button "确认" [disabled=false]
`);

await page.getByRole('button', { name: '确认' }).click();

VII. Conclusion

As a test automation engineer, mastering W3C ARIA Roles and applying them effectively in Playwright testing brings multiple benefits:

  1. Improved test stability: location based on semantic roles is more reliable than location based on implementation details
  2. Enhanced accessibility: ensure the application complies with WCAG standards and serves a broader user base
  3. Simplified test maintenance: when UI styles change, role-based tests usually do not need updating
  4. Cross-platform testing support: ARIA Roles behave consistently across different browsers and devices

By combining Playwright’s ARIA locators, state verification, and snapshot testing features, you can build a robust, maintainable, and accessibility-conscious automated test suite. As web applications grow increasingly complex, the importance of ARIA Roles in test automation will continue to grow, making them one of the core skills that modern web test engineers must master.

V. Implementation Recommendations and Challenges

5.1 Adoption Roadmap

  1. Foundation phase:

    • Gradually introduce the getByRole locator into existing tests
    • Add ARIA snapshot comparisons

  2. Advanced phase:

    • Build a role-driven test case library
    • Develop ARIA compliance monitoring

  3. AI integration phase:

    • Train a dedicated role classification model

Challenge 1: Dynamic Role Assignment
