item.title: AI Testing, the Inevitable Path for Testing Teams
item.description:
This article is translated and adapted from the latest post on the well-known testing blog https://testguild.com/ and discusses a roadmap for systematically implementing and advancing AI testing within testing teams. It offers considerable reference value, so I am sharing it with you all.

AI Test Automation Is No Longer Optional

In today’s software testing field, artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer merely an option but a significant strategic advantage. AI-driven testing tools can automate everything from test case generation to test execution, enabling your team to focus on delivering higher-quality software releases.

Tal Barmeir, CEO of Blinq.io, once noted: “The role of generative AI is to help us truly solve the problem of a massive backlog of testing demand with very limited coverage—a phenomenon we see across every industry.”

AI-driven testing tools can automate the entire process from test case creation to execution and maintenance, helping testing teams:

  • Reduce test creation time by up to 80%
  • Lower test maintenance costs by 40-60%
  • Accelerate time to market through faster release cycles
  • Improve test coverage across browsers, devices, and environments
  • Free up valuable engineering resources for innovation

This guide offers a structured approach to implementing AI testing, designed to deliver both immediate benefits and long-term transformation.

Phase 1 (Days 1-15) - Define Your AI Testing Strategy

Before diving into specific tools, you first need to clarify how you want to apply AI:

  • Assistive AI: Enhances human-led testing processes.
  • Autonomous AI: Test automation driven entirely by AI, with human oversight.

“Most organizations start with assistive AI. But they soon realize its value is limited and try to move to fully AI-led. That shift requires different tools, structures, and mindsets.”

For decision-making leaders of testing teams, the key strategic decisions include:

  • Scope of automation: Is your team automating existing test cases, or allowing AI to take full charge of creating, executing, and maintaining test scripts?

  • Integration requirements: How will AI testing integrate with your existing CI/CD pipelines and development workflows?

  • Success metrics: Which KPIs will be used to measure success (such as test coverage, execution time, defect detection, and so on)?

  • Risk assessment: Which applications or features are best suited as the initial targets for AI testing implementation?

Action recommendation: Before evaluating tools, be sure to define your AI testing vision, scope, and success criteria.

Phase 2 (Days 16-30) - Redefine QA Roles and Test Inputs

AI test automation does not eliminate existing roles; rather, it transforms them.

Traditional Role AI-Augmented Role Key Responsibilities
Manual Tester Prompt Engineer Create effective test prompts, review AI-generated tests
Automation Engineer AI Testing Lead Oversee the generation, execution, and maintenance of AI tests
QA Manager AI Testing Strategist Define AI testing strategy, measure ROI, optimize processes

“People often think AI means job losses. That is not the case. What it really does is redeploy testers—manual testers become prompt engineers, and automation engineers become supervisors of AI work.”

Expand Test Input Sources

AI testing platforms can generate comprehensive test cases from a variety of inputs, including:

  • Jira tickets and user stories
  • Screen recordings of application usage
  • Natural language requirements
  • API specifications and documentation
  • Existing manual test cases

This flexibility means AI testing does not need to strictly adhere to a BDD framework or a specific test case format, making AI testing accessible to teams at every maturity level.

Phase 3 (Days 31-45) - Evaluate AI Testing Tools

Choosing the right AI testing tool requires aligning it with your infrastructure, team skills, and long-term vision.

Core Capabilities of Enterprise AI Testing Platforms

  • Open-source test code generation: Generates maintainable code in standard frameworks (such as Playwright, Selenium, and so on).
  • Self-healing capability: Automatically adapts to user interface (UI) changes without human intervention.
  • Comprehensive test support: Covers functional, visual, performance, and security testing.
  • Enterprise integration: Works with your CI/CD pipelines, test management, and defect tracking systems.
  • Cross-platform testing: Supports web, mobile, API, and enterprise applications (such as Salesforce, SAP, and so on).
  • Visual testing: AI-driven visual comparison and anomaly detection.
  • Flaky test management: Automatically identifies and resolves inconsistent tests.

“Even if you stop using a particular vendor, you still have a code project you can maintain. No black box, no vendor lock-in.”

Decision framework: Evaluate tools against your specific needs, existing infrastructure, and team capabilities. Give priority to platforms that generate standard, maintainable test code rather than proprietary formats.

Phase 4 (Days 46-60) - Train for New AI-Augmented Testing Roles

Introducing AI into test automation brings new AI capabilities and responsibilities, elevating the role of the QA team.

Key Skills for the AI Testing Era

  • Prompt engineering: Creating effective test prompts to generate comprehensive test coverage.
  • AI test review: Evaluating and refining AI-generated test scripts.
  • Test maintenance management: Overseeing self-healing capabilities and test stability.
  • Test prioritization: Determining which tests deliver the highest value in each release.
  • Exploratory testing: Concentrating human creativity on edge cases and complex scenarios.

“The old skills were scripting and debugging. The new skills? Writing prompts, reviewing AI suggestions, and managing code at scale.”

Training Resources for the QA Team:

  • Internal workshops on AI testing concepts and prompt engineering.
  • Vendor-provided training on specific AI testing platforms.
  • Hands-on practice in real application testing scenarios.
  • Cross-training between manual and automation testers.

Leadership focus: Encourage experimentation and create a learning environment where the team can develop AI testing expertise through real-world application.

Phase 5 (Days 61-75) - Pilot and Expand AI Testing Coverage

Launch a focused pilot project using 10-20 test scenarios to achieve fast, measurable impact and build confidence in AI testing capabilities.

Ideal Pilot Project Characteristics:

  • An application of moderate complexity with a stable UI.
  • Existing manual test cases for comparison.
  • A regular release cadence to demonstrate CI/CD integration.
  • A mix of regression, functional, and visual testing needs.
  • Stakeholders who are open to innovation and process change.

Implementation Checklist:

  • Select the pilot application and define the test scope.
  • Configure the AI testing tool and integrate with CI/CD.
  • Create initial test prompts and generate baseline tests.
  • Execute tests across multiple environments.
  • Measure results against traditional testing methods.
  • Document lessons learned and optimization opportunities.

This phase is ideal for expanding test coverage across browsers, devices, and languages—leveraging the multilingual capabilities of AI models to efficiently test international applications.

Phase 6 (Days 76-90) - Measure KPIs and Optimize

Track key performance indicators (KPIs) to quantify the impact of AI testing implementation and uncover optimization opportunities.

Key AI Testing Metrics:

  • Release time: Reduction in overall test cycle time.
  • Test coverage: Increase in functional and platform coverage.
  • Maintenance effort: Reduction in test script maintenance time.
  • Defect detection: Increase in the defect identification rate.
  • Resource utilization: The QA team shifting focus to higher-value activities.

“Most leaders think AI testing is about cutting costs. But the biggest ROI is actually faster time to market.”

Continuous Improvement Framework:

  • Review AI testing performance and accuracy weekly.
  • Refine prompts based on test results and missed scenarios.
  • Extend AI testing to other applications and test types.
  • Document best practices and share them across teams.
  • Establish an AI testing center of excellence.

These insights will support your team in making data-driven decisions about test coverage, release readiness, and quality improvement.

Summary - Your 90-Day AI Testing Implementation Roadmap

Phase Timeline Focus Key Deliverables
1 Days 1-15 Strategy definition AI testing vision, implementation approach, success metrics
2 Days 16-30 Role transformation Updated team structure, skill requirements, input sources
3 Days 31-45 Tool selection AI testing platform evaluation, selection criteria, proof of concept
4 Days 46-60 Team training Skill development plan, training resources, knowledge sharing
5 Days 61-75 Pilot implementation Initial AI test suite, CI/CD integration, baseline metrics
6 Days 76-90 Measurement and optimization Performance analysis, optimization plan, scaling strategy

The Future of QA - AI-Driven Testing Leadership

With the right AI testing strategy, your QA organization will not only keep pace with the industry but will lead the transformation toward faster, more reliable software delivery. You are not merely automating tests; you are empowering your team to enhance and streamline the entire testing lifecycle, delivering higher-quality software at unprecedented speed while reducing risk and technical debt. Embrace AI testing now, and you will position your organization at the forefront of quality engineering, creating a sustainable competitive advantage through superior software quality and accelerated innovation.

item.title: Translated - Eight Major Test Automation Trends for 2025
item.description:
This article comes from TestGuild’s analysis in January of this year’s testing development trends. So far, its judgments still appear objective and accurate, so I am sharing the translation with everyone.

As we enter 2025, I believe the following test automation trends will profoundly influence the future of software testing.

Table of Contents

  • 1. AI Agent - The New Wave of Testing
  • 2. Shift-Right AI - Understanding Users
  • 3. QA for Everyone - Human-AI Collaboration
  • 4. The Evolving Tester Role - Adapting to the Future
  • 5. DevOps and SRE Integration - Continuous Quality
  • 6. End-to-End (E2E) Autonomous Quality Platforms
  • 7. Playwright - The Preferred Automation Tool
  • 8. Must-Know Programming Languages for Testers in 2025
  • Conclusion - The Path to Test Automation Success in 2025

AI Agent - The New Wave of Testing

I believe 2025 will witness the continued expansion of AI-assisted testing.

Why is that?

The use of AI in testing is growing exponentially: surveys show that, as of 2024, 72.3% of teams are actively exploring or adopting AI-driven testing workflows, whereas just a few years ago this technology was still in the early-adoption stage. This trend marks the fastest technology adoption curve in the history of our TestGuild test automation survey.

Building on the multimodal AI of 2024 (which processes multiple data types through specialized algorithms), the emerging trend is agentic AI.

First, you may ask: what exactly is agentic AI?

Such systems can operate autonomously, handling tasks that previously required human intervention. They can communicate, maintain long-term state, and make independent decisions based on interactions — essentially acting as a highly efficient team of testing assistants.

Still not clear? Let us illustrate with an example.

Example of an Agentic AI Test Automation Workflow

Imagine a real-world scenario: agentic AI autonomously manages the full regression test suite for a large e-commerce platform.

Rather than relying on pre-set scripts and fixed schedules, this agentic AI system will perform the following operations:

  • Priority determination: analyze recent code changes and feature releases, and rank regression tests according to the risk level of the modifications
  • Test selection and adaptation: dynamically select appropriate test cases, filtering a subset from the full suite based on risk assessment
  • Test execution and environment management: schedule test execution across multiple environments (browser/OS/device). If a test fails, automatically trigger diagnostic tests to collect detailed information, and even attempt to auto-fix simple issues
  • Result analysis and reporting: classify the severity of failures, identify patterns, and suggest fixes based on common error patterns
  • Feedback loop and continuous improvement: continuously self-optimize through accumulated experience

This vision is no fantasy. Survey data shows that teams are not only pursuing task automation but also relying on AI to make autonomous decisions — which is precisely the core of agentic AI:

  • Decision-making capability: AI tools are increasingly trusted to optimize test coverage and maintenance
  • Autonomy: interest in AI-driven pipelines and frameworks indicates that teams need solutions that minimize human intervention
  • Performance: the focus on AI-powered tools and frameworks signals a shift toward systems that learn and adapt dynamically

The pace of transformation has exceeded expectations: a webinar poll showed that 56% of teams are in the “research phase” of AI adoption, while 38% of enterprises see AI as a solution to the shortage of testing talent.

The views of industry giants are consistent with this (the author extends them here to the field of test automation):

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella recently mentioned AI “agents” will transform SaaS, achieving breakthroughs by handling complex tasks, learning continuously, and connecting seamlessly across systems. Experiments by Stanford researchers on AI agents replicating human behavior likewise confirm the potential of agentic AI to change the way we test.

Shift-Right AI - Understanding Users

Understanding real user behavior has become a core element of quality strategy in 2025. By analyzing user interactions in production environments, teams can discover patterns, predict problems, and ensure the software meets user expectations. The integration of AI enables teams to explore new paths for improving quality.

Survey data shows a marked increase in attention to predictive models and user behavior analysis, with teams focusing on using AI to uncover long-tail cases and refine their understanding of the user journey. Gojko Adzic envisions tools integrated directly into platforms, providing experience analytics and predictive models that proactively anticipate problems. This is especially valuable when managing massive volumes of user data (including long-tail cases), where AI plays a key role in identifying data patterns.

This shift-right approach complements traditional shift-left methodologies by emphasizing quality assurance after deployment. Potential benefits include:

  • Reduce user-reported defects through proactive monitoring
  • Improve feature adoption by optimizing high-value user flows
  • Improve test coverage through data-driven decisions based on real usage patterns

QA for Everyone - Human-AI Collaboration

With the adoption of agentic AI and end-to-end autonomous quality platforms (described in detail below), software testing will undergo dramatic changes in 2025. Low-code/no-code tools combined with AI allow testing to break through traditional barriers, enabling business analysts, developers, and even stakeholders without a technical background to participate in quality assurance. A webinar poll showed that 74% of participants considered themselves AI beginners, highlighting the need for tools that lower the barrier to entry.

Intuitive low-code solutions reduce the learning curve and accelerate tool adoption by automating complex tasks such as test creation and defect detection. Surveys show that 32.3% of teams are actively experimenting with no-code testing solutions.

At the same time, human oversight remains indispensable. As Tobias Müller put it: “The point is no longer whether to trust AI, but setting boundaries and trusting the rules you have set.” Teams that combine human experience with AI demonstrate better defect detection and faster testing cycles, proving the importance of human-AI collaboration.

The Evolving Tester Role - Adapting to the Future

Testers are transforming into hybrid roles that blend traditional skills with AI, DevOps, and automation knowledge. Survey data confirms this shift:

  • 45% of teams emphasize the need for AI skills
  • 51.8% prioritize DevOps knowledge
  • 72.3% focus on automation expertise

DevOps and SRE Integration - Continuous Quality

The integration of testing with DevOps and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practices is the most significant test automation trend of 2025. As enterprises place growing emphasis on continuous delivery and operational resilience, testing is evolving into a proactive quality assurance activity that runs throughout the software lifecycle.

Survey data reveals a significant shift: as of 2024, 51.8% of teams had adopted DevOps practices (only 16.9% in 2022). This growth confirms the deep integration of testing with DevOps/SRE workflows to safeguard software quality under high-speed delivery.

This integration goes beyond traditional QA, turning it into a continuous activity that improves the entire lifecycle and helping enterprises to:

  • Accelerate feedback loops: embed testing into CI/CD pipelines to detect issues immediately
  • Implement proactive quality assurance: integrate performance testing and monitoring into workflows to identify risks early
  • Foster team collaboration: shared quality ownership improves collaboration among QA, development, and operations teams

Survey data clearly supports this trend. From pipeline automation to performance monitoring, teams are adopting continuous quality practices aligned with operational excellence goals. If your organization has not yet integrated testing with DevOps/SRE, 2025 is the perfect time to make the transition.

End-to-End (E2E) Autonomous Quality Platforms

E2E platforms are becoming the core of testing strategy. These platforms integrate testing, usability, performance, accessibility, and security within a unified framework to address a broader range of quality concerns. By using AI to automate the testing lifecycle, teams report significant improvements in defect detection and test coverage.

Survey data shows significant growth:

  • Security testing grew from 8.2% in 2021 to 39.5% in 2024
  • Performance testing adoption reached 41%
  • API testing grew from 13.1% in 2021 to 46.2% in 2024

These metrics reflect the growing reliance of enterprises on comprehensive quality platforms to manage all their testing needs.

Playwright - The Preferred Automation Tool

As I predicted last year, Playwright has become the tool of choice for many testers. According to the analysis in Playwright Surpasses Cypress (Future Outlook), this prediction has been validated.

What about current progress? Thanks to outstanding versatility, reliability, and performance, Playwright continues to consolidate its leading position in 2025. The TestGuild 2024 survey and community feedback show its remarkable growth.

Testing tool preferences have undergone a major shift (based on an analysis of 2018-2024 data):

  • Playwright: a 45.1% adoption rate makes it the fastest-growing tool, with advantages including cross-browser support, API testing capability, and efficient workflows
  • Selenium: once the market leader, its adoption rate has now dropped to 22.1% as teams pursue more efficient and stable solutions
  • Cypress: holding its ground in front-end testing, it maintains a stable user base of 14.4%

Playwright users commonly report:

  • Faster test execution: accelerating feedback loops and improving the development lifecycle
  • Lower test flakiness: producing more stable and reliable test results

Beyond its initial UI browser automation capabilities, Playwright has evolved to support advanced features such as API testing, making it a comprehensive solution for modern testing needs.

Must-Know Programming Languages for Testers in 2025

According to the TIOBE Programming Community Index, Python has topped the list for two consecutive years. This matches my expectation — thanks to its simplicity, strong library support, and dominance in AI/machine learning, Python remains the preferred language for testers in 2025. Whether you are just starting out in automation or are a seasoned testing expert, Python is the bridge connecting today’s challenges with the future possibilities of test automation.

Conclusion - The Path to Test Automation Success in 2025

2025 will be a pivotal turning point for software testing, offering unprecedented opportunities for those who embrace change. The convergence of AI maturity, team collaboration, and tool evolution marks the dawn of a new era in quality assurance.

Success requires not only paying attention to trends but also taking action:

  • Embrace agentic AI: explore how autonomous AI agents can optimize workflows and reduce human intervention
  • Adopt shift-right testing practices: balance traditional shift-left approaches with post-deployment monitoring to ensure the software meets real user expectations
  • Invest in skills development: equip your team with AI, automation, and DevOps knowledge to stay competitive
  • Integrate testing with DevOps/SRE: break down silos and embed quality assurance into every stage of delivery
  • Make good use of comprehensive tools: from Playwright to Python, choose tools that meet current needs and are future-ready

These trends signal a fundamental shift in how quality assurance is approached. As the boundaries between testing, development, and operations blur, the role of the modern tester is evolving into a strategic one. To gain a deeper grasp of these transformative trends, join the annual Automation Guild conference and help shape the future of testing together with industry leaders.

item.title: Ten Misconceptions That Make Testers Harm Quality
item.description:
Many companies call the engineers who perform testing QA (quality assurance), but QA and Tester are actually two different roles. Even so, there is no denying that a test engineer’s primary responsibility is also oriented toward quality — helping the team improve quality by assessing the state of quality.

But even so, is a test engineer’s work necessarily helpful to quality improvement? In real work, some misconceptions can instead make testers’ work have a negative impact on quality.

Here Qiucao has sorted out and summarized ten misconceptions by which testers may harm quality, along with the corresponding correct practices.

1. Testing’s job is to find and report Bugs, but not to confirm them

Misconception: Developers and testers often argue over whether a certain issue should be reported as a Bug. “The requirement doesn’t ask for it,” “this issue doesn’t affect users,” and similar reasons come up all the time. Many testers do stop reporting such issues because of these reasons, and some even check with developers whether they are allowed to file a Bug before reporting it.

This is a misconception that does great harm to quality. The value of testing lies in assessing the state of quality, and the key to assessment is independence. Quality is not about right or wrong, only about good or bad. A behavior not defined in the requirements does not mean it is unwanted; not affecting users does not mean it is a good implementation. Testing stands from the perspective of assessing quality, so pointing out defects or raising suggestions for improvement is part of the job. Developers are responsible for analyzing, confirming, and fixing defects. If developers and testers disagree on the confirmation, the PO, business analysts, or CCB members can arbitrate.

But for testers, reporting every product behavior that they feel is problematic or of poor quality is a professional obligation. Deliberately or inadvertently hiding or covering up defects is the real harm to product quality.

2. Finding a Bug is only the beginning; we should also provide as much context as possible for fixing it

Misconception: Some testers think that once they have found a problem and reported it, their work is done, that the subsequent fixing process has nothing to do with them, and that all they need to do is verify it after the fix

Testing is one link in the entire software product development lifecycle, and it ultimately serves the overall quality of the product. The Bug itself, in fact, has no value for the product, because only a Bug that has been resolved helps product quality. From this perspective, although reporting Bugs is a tester’s main job, for the product the ultimate goal is to resolve the Bug. So as one part of product development, even though fixing Bugs is not directly the tester’s responsibility, we should still provide the necessary support for resolving them.

This part was discussed in detail in a previous article 【】, which you may refer to if interested.

3. Testing is not just about verifying requirements

Misconception: Testing only needs to verify that the parts explicitly defined in the requirements are correct; undefined parts need not be tested

This is somewhat related to the first misconception and is the premise of many developer–tester arguments about bugs. In the earlier article 【】 on misconceptions about testing goals, we also mentioned this point: beyond verifying requirements, testing should cover much more exploratory work. Testing is not merely checking.

Beyond that, here I want to emphasize even more the integrity and systematic nature of the product. Especially in an agile development model, this misconception is easily amplified.

In agile, the output of an agile iteration is the Increment (product increment), which holds true for development work. But testing work is oriented toward the entire product system and cannot cover only the increment. Requirements are incremental too, so of course testing cannot cover only the requirements of the increment. This is why regression testing is a category that must be included in testing, and it is also the fundamental reason test automation is receiving more and more attention. (For analysis and introductions related to agile, see the earlier agile series.)

4. Testing is endless; use good steel on the blade’s edge

Misconception: To find more Bugs, explore and diverge as much as possible, and exploit the clustering effect of Bugs to discover as many Bugs as possible

Still in the article 【】, we also clarified that the goal of testing is not to find more Bugs either. Moreover, testing is in fact endless; the ultimate purpose of testing is to provide a reliable, complete assessment of the quality state of the whole product or system. And whether this quality state is objective and accurate is not necessarily positively correlated with the number of Bugs.

While finding as many Bugs as possible, testers also need to recognize that we are systematically assessing quality, yet testing can never be exhaustive. Therefore we must allocate our limited time scientifically, giving priority to high-priority parts — new features, code changes, and high-risk modules are all parts that should be tested first and given key assurance.

Precision Testing and Risk-Based Testing (RBT) are practices under this way of thinking that put our testing resources and time first into the high-value parts.

5. Testing work does not begin only at the test-submission stage; it starts as early as product requirement discussions

Misconception: Testing should formally begin only after the product is submitted for testing, and Bugs should also be reported only after submission

Today, the above misconception is of course incorrect, because both shift-left testing and various testing theories emphasize the importance of early testing involvement.

But theory is theory; in actual practice, testing usually still really begins only after submission for testing.

On one hand, in the early stage of a product, testing has a low presence and low participation and is easily overlooked;

on the other hand, many testing teams are assessed heavily on the number of Bugs, which further erodes the motivation for early testing involvement and makes testers less willing to help the team expose product problems early.

But from the perspective of product delivery, the later the stage, the higher the cost of fixing a problem. So from a product management standpoint, we should abandon the orientation of assessing by Bug count and guide active early participation by testing. Testing can bring its sensitivity to problems into play, identifying and considering many exceptional scenarios starting from requirement discussions, and helping the team avoid them in advance.

6. In design and architecture discussions, testing should not be invisible

Misconception: Architecture and system design, as well as detailed design, are the development team’s tasks; testers need not understand or participate in the discussions and can simply wait until product development is complete and then test against the requirements

Similar to the previous point, shift-left testing does not merely mean that testers understand requirements better; it also requires testers to participate in design and even coding stages.

We must return to the goal of testing: to assess the quality state of the product as accurately as possible. And quality is necessarily closely tied to the concrete implementation of the product; the more clearly we understand the implementation details, the more targeted our testing can be, including helping the team avoid quality problems in advance during the design and coding stages.

Conversely, if design and code are a complete black box, it is very likely that some key test scenarios will be missed and problems will leak through.

  • Without understanding how load balancing is implemented in a cloud application, verifying only on a single node makes it impossible to catch problems caused by load-balancing failures
  • Without understanding the system’s caching implementation, it is hard to purposefully construct cache-hit scenarios
  • Without understanding the responsive layout implementation of the UI, it is hard to efficiently carry out compatibility testing
  • Without understanding the interface’s validation mechanism, it is hard to construct effective API test data

All of the above show that testing should not stay outside the design stage and treat product design as outside the scope of testing, thereby ignoring participation in this stage.

7. An independent test environment is a prerequisite for adequate testing

Misconception: Test execution only needs to focus on the product itself; testing can be done on an integration environment or even a development environment without affecting test results

It is true that the object of testing is the product itself. But the test environment is actually a key constraint on whether the product can be tested comprehensively and efficiently.

In software testing and exploration, using the product usually involves the superposition of many different operations and interactions. And when discovering product problems, an important prerequisite for judging the problem is that the relevant preconditions and associated factors of the product itself are clear and definite. To ensure this, an independent, interference-free test environment is especially necessary. If a development environment is used for testing, developers are simultaneously debugging and making changes on that environment during testing, which not only produces a large number of invalid issues but is also a great waste of resources for testing, problem localization, and the like.

Beyond that, testing inevitably involves creating various exceptional scenarios, and an independent test environment makes it easier for testers to adjust different test scenarios, such as:

  • Modifying network configurations to create scenarios such as proxy access, internal and external IPs, and weak networks
  • Modifying the system time, triggering scheduled tasks, simulating data for different time periods, and similar scenarios
  • Simulating scenarios such as insufficient resources, full disk space, and massive or huge files
  • Some limiting factors in the product, enabling Debug mode, different authentication settings, and various configuration changes

All these tests are built on the foundation of an independent, controllable test environment.

8. Test automation code is also a program; treat test code the way you treat the product

Misconception: Writing test automation is simply to replace part of manual test execution; once the automation code is written and can run and cover the relevant cases, that is enough

The purpose of test automation is indeed to replace a great deal of manual testing work and achieve efficiency gains. But implementing test automation is not a one-off deal; it is also a long-term process. Moreover, test automation itself is implemented through program code, and where there is a program there will be bugs, so quality assurance and maintenance of the automation scripts and tools themselves is also an important part of a tester’s job.

It is not the case that writing a runnable automation script means we have “done automation.” Automation scripts, like software products, should go through a lifecycle of requirements analysis, design, coding, testing, and subsequent maintenance.

So test automation itself is also a fairly large investment. For the relevant scripts to keep delivering value over the long term and truly achieve the goal of improving execution efficiency, good design and continuous maintenance of the test automation code are indispensable.

9. CI/CD pipelines are also testing’s responsibility

Misconception: CI/CD, as infrastructure for many development teams today, is usually built and maintained by dedicated DevOps engineers; as testers, we only need to write the automation scripts for the testing portion

Admittedly, within the entire CI/CD pipeline, the part directly related to testing is mainly test automation. But again: testing, as a member of the whole development process, cannot exist independently of that process. Especially in agile development, the integrity of the team is emphasized even more, and the team as a whole is responsible for the development process.

Therefore, in the process of establishing, operating, and keeping the CI/CD pipeline flowing, there is no clear notion that testing is only responsible for the test automation stage.

As professionals with a quality perspective, we can also play a greater role in building the CI/CD pipeline:

  • Defining quality gates for the flow between stages in the pipeline, reflecting shift-left testing in the CI/CD pipeline
  • Controlling and identifying code changes, which is highly significant for precision testing in the testing phase
  • Monitoring of development, integration, test, and even online production environments, especially the collection and implementation of many quality-related metrics
  • Visualization, including automated test reports and the status presentation of various data tracking

10. Cherish every opportunity to understand end users’ usage scenarios

Misconception: As a member of the development team, testing need not proactively engage with end users. Interfacing with users is more the job of the sales, after-sales, and customer service teams

Testing work is oriented toward quality, and the ultimate judge of quality is in fact the end user. So many teams emphasize that testing is the voice of the end user, a role that uses and experiences the product from the user’s perspective and discovers problems in advance.

Therefore, in this sense, testing should actually engage with users more, understanding the different scenarios, demands, and even preferences with which users use the product.

So, when there is an opportunity to engage with users, testing should be proactive rather than resistant. As testers, there are quite a few such opportunities; make full use of chances to engage with users to enrich our understanding of the industry the product belongs to and apply it to our testing work.

  • User issue support. When some customer issues fed back to the development team require technical support, testers often need to face customers directly, and this is also a place where we intuitively understand users’ usage scenarios of the product and the problems they face.
  • External testing. Before choosing a product, many users will have acceptance testing for it. These tests are often carried out on the customer’s side, but product testers often provide support or perform testing as the product side, which is field testing. This is also a great window for deeply understanding user scenarios
  • Customer visits. Some companies arrange visits and interviews with end customers in the early or middle stages of product development, and sometimes invite the development team to participate. Although in most cases roles such as system analysts and architects participate more, testing also takes part in such visits, which is an excellent opportunity to deeply understand product application scenarios at an early stage.
  • Industry reports. Besides direct communication with end customers, paying attention to industry reports, news, and trend analyses for the industry the product belongs to is likewise an excellent channel for deeply understanding the industry and users the product serves.

The above is a summary of the ten misconceptions by which testers harm quality; everyone is welcome to discuss and add to them. In addition, for Qiucao’s course on systematically improving testing skills, you can reply with “Outline” or check the course catalog in the official account menu.

item.title: Software Testing in the AI Era - Assistant or Adversary?
item.description:
In the present era, the AI wave is sweeping in, and “the future is already here” is no longer an empty slogan. AI-related topics and discussions have become the sure-fire “traffic magnet” of the tech world; from autonomous driving to intelligent customer service, every industry seems eager to ride this wave of AI hype.

But as testing professionals, when we face the rapid development of AI, what we care about most is probably this: What can AI actually do in software testing? Can it really help us improve output and efficiency? Or, as it evolves, will AI completely replace testing roles?

In this article, let us explore this topic.

The Role of AI in the Different Stages of Software Testing

AI testing, when it comes down to it, is about having AI take on part of, assist with, or enhance the original testing work. In other words, AI itself does not change the underlying laws of the software testing lifecycle within software development.

Therefore, we can look at what role AI can play from the perspective of the different stages of the software testing lifecycle and the scope of testing responsibilities.

Requirements Analysis Stage

At this stage, we can use AI’s natural language processing technology to sort out the original requirements documents and produce analysis results including business flowcharts, operation flowcharts, and data flow diagrams.

At the same time, we can combine more relevant local data — such as historical bug data, test logs, and project data — to identify testing priorities, build risk models, and detect risks. Based on these analysis results, we can then help formulate a more reasonable test plan.

Test Case Design Stage

During the software design and development phase, testers usually complete test design in parallel. At this stage, we can leverage AI to help us generate test cases based on the requirements documents and the results of the requirements analysis phase. With AI, we can produce more and fuller positive and negative cases as well as a variety of boundary conditions to expand coverage.

Test Preparation Stage

At this stage, the main work is setting up and deploying the test environment. We can use AI capabilities combined with a CI platform to achieve intelligent management of test servers and database environments, as well as the dynamic allocation of resources.

Test Execution Stage

During the execution stage, we can dynamically adjust the test order based on factors such as various risk assessments, dependencies, and business impact, prioritizing coverage of higher-risk modules so as to expose defects as early as possible.

In addition, AI can enhance capabilities such as log analysis and image comparison, improving our test execution efficiency and defect detection ability.

Test Reporting Stage

In the closing part of testing, using AI to perform comprehensive analysis of various process data can help us produce multi-dimensional test reports, providing project decision-makers with a structured analysis of testing status.

How AI Empowers Software Testing at This Stage

The current development of AI can already provide more support in many typical testing scenarios. The following outlines some typical scenarios that can be empowered by AI:

  • Intelligent Data Generation - Create diverse datasets covering common scenarios and edge cases
  • Test Automation - Automatically adapt to UI changes to keep automation scripts stable
  • Precise Regression Testing - Intelligently select related test cases based on code changes
  • Process Cloning - Learn testing workflows and then automatically execute similar processes
  • Dynamic Waiting Mechanism - Intelligently judge page load status before performing actions
  • Intelligent Log Analysis - Analyze and identify potential problem patterns in error logs
  • Load / Performance Testing - Simulate real user behavior and diagnose performance bottlenecks
  • Continuous Test Monitoring - Monitor application status in real time and alert on anomalies
  • Exploratory Testing Support - Provide intelligent suggestions during exploratory testing
  • Predictive Analysis - Predict release risks based on historical data

The Advantages of Introducing AI

AI can keep learning, training, and improving continuously, so after introducing AI, we can build advantages across many of the following aspects:

  • Cost Optimization - Reduce labor costs, optimize resource allocation, and speed up time to market
  • Stable and Reliable - Ensure standardized test execution and result consistency
  • Early Defect Screening - Expose problems early and shorten the fix cycle
  • Fast Feedback - Run tests in parallel across multiple environments to shorten the feedback loop
  • High-Quality Cases - Automatically generate diverse cases such as unit tests, regression tests, and API tests

Significant Challenges Still Remain in Applying AI

Artificial Intelligence or “Artificial Stupidity”?

If AI’s training data is biased, the results can be so absurd that they make you question reality. If the training outcome of AI is not ideal, then applying AI may not only fail to improve efficiency, but also waste a large amount of extra resources correcting its execution results.

Data Dependency Syndrome

AI’s high demands for quality training data and various parameter adjustments often impose significant constraints on real-world deployment in specific industries.

Maintenance Costs Are Higher Than You Think

Beyond the investment in data resources, training models on local datasets also requires a great deal of time and money, including equipment resources, which are a considerable expense. In addition, the current shortage of AI talent makes the labor cost of AI applications much higher.

Experience and Intuition Are Things AI Can Never Learn

Veteran testers with rich experience can sniff out hidden defects in a product from all kinds of subtle clues; this “mystical,” sixth-sense-like ability is bound to be difficult for AI to replicate.

Assistant or Adversary?

“With AI developing like this, are test engineers going to lose their jobs?” There is really no need to panic!

AI is still essentially a tool. Just as test automation replaced some manual checks, it only changes parts of the way we work rather than eliminating the role altogether. Future testers will be more like an “AI Trainer + Strategy Commander” — what we actually need to do boils down to the following:

  • Teach AI to understand business logic (for example, what a “correct order status transition” is);
  • Design smarter testing strategies (for example, how to balance automation and exploratory testing);
  • Interpret AI’s results and make decisions (for example, whether a given anomaly is a bug or a false positive).

AI is like a robotic vacuum: it can help you clean the floor, but when it comes to stubborn stains (complex business scenarios) or changes in furniture layout (requirement changes), you still have to step in yourself.

Conclusion - AI Is Not the End, but a New Starting Point

The application of AI in software testing is still in its infancy. We can see its enormous potential, but it is not yet time to place full trust in it and abandon the original models. As testers, rather than worrying about “whether we will be replaced,” it is better to actively embrace change: learn some basic machine learning, get to know mainstream AI testing tools, and even take part in training your own models.

After all, in the future world of software testing, the most sought-after people will certainly not be “those who are best at clicking a mouse,” but “those who are best at working with AI”. What do you think?

Some earlier articles also discussed the development of AI. For further reading:

In the AI Era, Do Programmers Still Have a Future?

The Testing Profession and Its Future Prospects

With the rapid development of AI technology, from ChatGPT to the explosion of DeepSeek, AI can now genuinely play a role in assisting our daily work.

Beyond specific areas such as assisted programming and copywriting, we can also make full use of AI’s powerful logical capabilities and vast foundational data to help us propose practical and feasible improvement plans for some of the difficulties we encounter at work.

But for AI to give us actionable solutions, the design of the prompt framework and the contextual information provided to AI are extremely critical. A well-designed prompt framework can help us quickly obtain highly valuable references.

A Case of the Predicament We Face

Here we use a fairly common case of an agile team’s quality predicament to illustrate:

As a test engineer responsible for quality assurance in an agile team running the Scrum framework, the team also includes an SM, a PO, two Android developers (among whom Xiao Li is responsible for the overall system design of the App), one back-end developer, and one part-time visual designer. The team’s product is a companion Android App for an IoT smart bracelet product. However, due to issues such as coordination with the hardware team, frequently changing requirements, untimely visual design, delayed test submissions, and a backlog of bugs, product quality is not optimistic. The App has now gone through multiple iterations, and the planned launch date is drawing ever closer. How can we propose an improvement plan for the current quality predicament?

Designing the Prompt Framework

For AI to help us produce a feasible improvement plan, we first need to design the prompt framework reasonably, so that the final plan better fits the team’s current situation and is actionable.

The key points of the prompt framework design are then:

  • A given role, so that AI determines from what perspective to propose the improvement plan
  • The current status quo, that is, sufficient background information and context
  • What AI should analyze in detail, or what its task should be
  • The specific output expected from AI, including format requirements and the elements to be included

item.title: Some Pitfalls in Software Testing - Things We Can Do but Should Not Do
item.description:
8 Kinds of Work in Software Testing That “We Can Do, but Should Not Do”

In software testing, we often face a problem - many tasks are indeed things we can accomplish, and doing them may seem perfectly natural, yet in many cases these efforts yield very little. These range from over-automation to frequently running unnecessary regression tests, to name a few.

As technology evolves, the tools available to testers let us accomplish far more, but that does not mean every choice is a wise one. Some tasks, when done blindly, tend to undermine the things that truly matter - output, efficiency, maintainability, and so on.

This article lists eight pieces of work in testing that “we can do, but should not do”. Sometimes, taking a step back is the smarter choice.

1. Automating All Tests

You can: Modern test automation tools let us automate almost any test case - from every click in the user interface to every API call - all of which can technically be driven through automation.

But you shouldn’t: Just because test automation is feasible does not mean it is the best choice. For example:

A product’s user interface is highly dynamic, with designers adjusting it every week. If you choose to automate every test, the relevant automated tests risk breaking after each UI change.

In this case, manual testing may be more effective.

2. Using Overly Complex Locators in Automation Scripts

You can: In automation tools such as Selenium and Playwright, XPath and CSS selectors let us pinpoint even the deepest elements on a page.

But you shouldn’t: Overly complex locators tend to make tests fragile. For example:

Using a complex XPath to locate a menu often causes multiple tests to fail once the development team refactors the HTML structure, forcing the team to spend a great deal of time on fixes.

At this point, other approaches may be more effective for the stability of automated cases, such as agreeing with the development team to add a test-id attribute to elements.

3. Running the Full Regression Suite on Every Commit

You can: In modern CI/CD pipelines, every code commit can easily trigger a full regression run.

But you shouldn’t: In practice, this is often excessive. Imagine a small code fix triggering the entire regression suite, a process that may take several hours or even longer.

For teams that have not raised automation coverage to a certain level, running a full regression after each commit is an even worse nightmare. The better approach is still to stay on top of what changed and implement precise testing based on the changes and their impact.

4. Over-Mocking in API Testing

You can: Mocking API responses can greatly speed up testing and remove dependencies on external services.

But you shouldn’t: Over-mocking, however, cuts us off from the real environment. A large number of Mock APIs can indeed improve debugging and verification efficiency, but they depart from what genuine testing requires. Testing in real scenarios is indispensable, just as we cannot anticipate every exception.

5. Writing Extremely Detailed Bug Reports for Trivial Issues

You can: With the help of assistive testing tools, we can catch many small defects in the UI layer, in prompt messages, and the like, and we can write extremely thorough bug reports following case specifications.

But you shouldn’t: Not every minor issue deserves an exhaustive, blow-by-blow report. The purpose of finding a bug is ultimately to fix the bug, not the bug itself, and the value of bugs also varies in importance. I once analyzed what makes a good bug report in 【】 - the value of a bug report lies in being a channel for communicating with developers; the boilerplate text of the report itself has no value.

6. Using AI to Generate Test Cases Without Human Supervision

You can: Advances in AI have actually made it possible to use AI tools to rapidly generate large numbers of test cases from requirements documents, covering a wide range of scenarios.

But you shouldn’t: Today’s AI, however, especially for a specific business domain, lacks human contextual understanding and the combined information gathered through various internal communications, which can lead to redundant cases or to missing critical test cases.

7. Using Too Many Assertions in a Test

You can: Combining automation tools with AI, we can indeed verify a large number of fields, properties, and UI elements within a single test.

But you shouldn’t: Too many assertions, however, only make a test huge and complex and hard to debug. When some assertions fail, it often takes a great deal of effort to track down the cause.

8. Executing Tests on Every Possible Device and Browser Combination

You can: For compatibility testing, modern cross-browser and cross-device testing tools let us run tests across many operating systems and devices.

But you shouldn’t: Testing every possible combination is neither necessary nor practical. The focus should be on covering the key scenarios that users actually use. Moreover, developments in engineering such as responsive design have greatly reduced the risk of compatibility issues.

Conclusion

In software testing, “being able to do it” does not always mean it is the best choice. We need to find a balance between technical capability and practical feasibility. By avoiding these “because we can” pitfalls and building a lean, efficient, and genuinely valuable test suite, we contribute far more meaningfully to product quality assurance.

Welcome to follow QiuCao for a steady stream of more hands-on technical content on software quality!

item.title: Can You Still Work in Testing Without Coding Skills
item.description:
Many people from non-IT backgrounds who want to switch to testing have heard it said that software testing has a low barrier to entry—that you can get into the industry even without knowing how to code. So is that actually the case?

The answer should be stated plainly:

Without coding skills, you actually can work in software testing—and yet, in practice, you actually cannot.

Why you actually can

Software testing is not a discipline built on coding ability, which is why, in principle, you can do it.

Software testing is the act of exposing quality problems in a product through testing; it is, in essence, a skill of discovering the unknown. What matters more, then, are abilities such as experimentation, exploration, observation, reasoning, questioning, and modeling. Having coding skills, on the other hand, mostly helps you understand how the product is implemented, or lets you use code to extend your testing methods and improve testing efficiency. In this sense, coding ability is a supporting capability—one that assists the testing work, but is by no means the decisive factor in whether that work can be accomplished!

In his paper “Testing and Checking”, James Bach elaborated on the relationship between testing and checking

testing is the broader concept, while checking is only a subset of testing—and checking itself is further divided into manual checking and checking performed with the help of machines (tools).

What coding ability affects, then, falls mostly within that tool-assisted checking part.

That is why, in the early days, many testing experts who excelled at the work were not particularly good at coding; more often than not, they were domain experts in the relevant business area, equipped with outstanding testing thinking—that is, the detective-like abilities of observation and reasoning mentioned above.

So, in truth, lacking coding skills does not prevent you from doing testing work exceptionally well.

Why you actually cannot

And yet, we must also say that, without coding skills, in practice you really cannot.

As we noted above, in the early days there were indeed testing experts who could not code. But times have changed, and the reality today is quite different. As the industry has evolved, the direction of the testing profession has arguably departed from its original track. It is rather lamentable, and worthy of a sigh!

There are several reasons:

The rise of development models that emphasize fast delivery, such as Agile

In Agile development models, there is in fact no longer a dedicated testing role; instead, the emphasis is on team members being versatile generalists who can take on a range of development tasks with one specialty and many skills—including both development and testing. As a member of the team, a tester naturally cannot do testing alone; when necessary, they must also be able to pick up development work, at least including tasks originally in the developer’s domain such as unit testing and integration testing. Coding ability is, of course, the hard requirement for meeting this condition.

The mandatory requirement for test automation skills

Also driven by the needs of development models such as Agile and continuous integration, test automation has become an indispensable part of the process. And as the foundational capability for test automation, coding ability is naturally a necessity.

But it must be pointed out here that something like test automation—aimed at “quickly completing testing”—is, according to the relationship between testing and checking shown in the figure above, not really “testing” at all; it is much more “checking”. A single-minded emphasis on coding ability is, in a sense, actually a weakening of the requirements of testing work—that is, it increasingly demands only “checking” rather than “testing”.

The talent market is oversupplied

Finally, there is the industry environment. In the early days of the internet boom, the talent gap was large, and a great deal of “verification” work was done manually by junior staff or complete beginners with zero foundation who did not need coding skills; manual “checking” accounted for a larger share.

But when the industry turns downward, companies cut costs, leading to an oversupplied talent market. The entry barrier naturally rises, job requirements climb accordingly, and expectations for tool-based “verification” grow higher—so coding ability, test automation, tool development, and the like have all but become must-have skills.

Layered on top of that is the current prevalence of development models such as Agile and the resulting demand for test automation. It is fair to say that, without coding skills, in today’s environment it has become very hard to argue that one can still work in testing—there is simply no way in.

Conclusion

So, under present conditions, when it comes to testing work, lacking coding skills does not mean you cannot accomplish the work—but without coding ability it has become very difficult to get on board.

Therefore, as individuals swept along by the tide of the times, what we can do is not to swim against the current, but to steadily build personal capabilities that move with the trend. But we must still understand what the core requirements of this work truly are—accumulate steadily and then burst forth, for gold only appears after all the sand is washed away!

item.title: Mastering Regular Expressions and Leaving the Beginner Stage Behind
item.description:
Preface

Regular Expression is a powerful language for describing text patterns. It uses concise combinations of symbols to describe complex string-matching rules. It is widely used in data validation, text extraction, log analysis, and other fields, and plays an important role in our daily work.

In the software industry, whether you have mastered regular expressions is often an important marker that separates a rookie from a veteran. In this article, we walk through the application of regular expressions with concrete examples so you can leave the beginner stage behind as soon as possible.

Core Syntax of Regular Expressions

To learn regular expressions, a very intuitive online validation platform is recommended here, https://regex101.com , which is very helpful for practicing and mastering regex syntax.

Ordinary Characters and Special Characters

A regular expression is a matching rule. Naturally, it can first match all kinds of ordinary characters, mainly Chinese and English words, letters, and digits. In addition, regular expressions reserve many special characters, such as * ? + . () [] $ ^ \ |, which represent special matching rules. When we need to treat these special characters as ordinary characters to be matched, we need to use the \ symbol to escape them, so \ is also called the escape character. For example, \? will match a ? character in the target text, and \\ will match a \ character in the target text

Quantifiers

Quantifiers are symbols used to control the number of matches:

  • * zero or more times (e.g. a* can match “”, “a”, “aa”)
  • + one or more times (a+ must have at least one a)
  • ? zero or one time (a? can match "" or a)
  • {n} matches exactly n times ({4} matches 4 times)
  • {m,n} matches m to n times (inclusive)
  • {m,} matches m or more times
  • {,n} matches zero to n times

In addition, there are two matching modes in regular expressions

  • Greedy mode: this is the default mode, which matches the longest possible run of characters that fit the rule in the target text
  • Lazy mode: if a ? is added after a quantifier, it marks a lazy match, that is, matching as few characters as possible that fit the rule

For example:

浮云长长长长长长长消

This couplet contains 7 长 characters. The regular expression 长{2,3}, in the default greedy mode, will match 长长长 2 times, while 长{2,3}? matches as few characters as possible and will match 长长 3 times

Metacharacters

Besides quantifiers, there is another class of metacharacters, the fundamental special symbols reserved to build regular expressions:

  • \d matches a digit (equivalent to [0-9])
  • \D matches a non-digit
  • \w matches a word character, including letters, digits, and underscore (equivalent to [A-Za-z0-9_])
  • \W matches a non-word character
  • \s matches a whitespace character (space/tab/newline)
  • \S matches a non-whitespace character
  • . matches any single character (by default it does not match a newline)
  • | means logical “or”

Position Anchors

Used to precisely locate the matching position:

  • \b matches a word boundary (e.g. \bcat\b matches a whole word)
  • \B matches a non-word-boundary
  • ^ matches the start of the target text, and in multiline mode also matches the start of a line
  • $ matches the end of the target text, and in multiline mode also matches the end of a line

For example: In tester is good at testing, using ^test will only match the test at the start of the line, but the test in testing will not be matched; and if test\b is used, it still matches nothing, because in this text test is never a standalone word and there is no word boundary after test

Character Classes

Character classes are used to batch-match a specific set of characters:

  • [abc] matches any one of a/b/c
  • [^abc] matches characters not in the set
  • Range notation: [a-z] (lowercase letters), [A-Z] (uppercase letters), [0-9] (digits)

In the following example, [b-f] matches only the d,e in the target string

Groups

Grouping is an important technique in regular expressions. It groups matching rules so that matched content can be extracted in subsequent text processing. A group is denoted by enclosing a pattern in () within the expression.

For example, specify a string

1

this is a "testtest" string to demo regex group!

Groups and Their References

Groups are numbered starting from 1 by default, that is, when there are multiple groups, they can be back-referenced in order with \1 \2

In this example, we specify two groups with (is)(\s)\1\2, group 1 matches “is”, group 2 matches a whitespace character (here a space), and then \1\2 references these two groups respectively; in effect it matches the case where "is"+space appears twice in a row

Marking a Group as Non-Capturing

When we group, if we do not want a certain group to be referenced later, we can use (?:pattern) to mark it, specifying that the current group will not be referenced later. This group is then ignored in the default capture numbering and is not assigned a number.

In the above example, if we specify that the second group is not to be referenced

1

(is)(?:\s)\1\2

Then the regular expression in the above example actually has a syntax error and cannot complete the match, because the second group is ignored while \2 references it, which causes a pattern error due to its absence

Adding Comments to Groups

For some complex regular expressions, we can also add comments to a group to explain the regular expression (?#comment)(other group)

Naming Groups

Besides referencing groups by their default numeric index, you can also name a group: (?P<name>pattern). Then reference it with (?P=<name>)

Based on the above, use the following regex as an illustration

1

(?#这是一个嵌套分组示例)(?P<demo>t(?:\w*)t)(?P=demo)

Assertions

Assertions are mainly used for judgment, to match the position of characters that fit a pattern. Because they mainly judge positions and do not consume characters, they are generally also called zero-width assertions

Assertions can be divided into 4 categories, still using the text from the above example

1

this is a "testtest" string to demo regex group!

Positive Lookahead Assertion

Judges that the characters after the matching position fit the pattern, asserted with (?=pattern)

Example:

Negative Lookahead Assertion

Judges that the characters after the matching position do not fit the given pattern, asserted with (?!pattern)

Example:

Positive Lookbehind and Negative Lookbehind Assertions

Opposite to lookahead, lookbehind assertions match whether the characters before the expected position fit a pattern, and also come in positive and negative forms. Adding a < after the ? indicates lookbehind, namely (?<=pattern) and (?<!pattern)

Matching Modes

Besides the main matching rules of regular expressions above, regular expressions also have some matching modes. They are represented by \ plus some special letters for different modes

  • \g indicates global matching, that is, it matches all qualifying substrings in the given text; if not specified, it only matches the first substring that fits the pattern
  • \m multiline mode, mainly specifies whether ^ $ match the start and end of a line
  • \i ignore case when matching
  • \x whether to ignore whitespace in our pattern text when matching, useful when writing more complex rules
  • \s specifies that . includes the newline character when matching characters
  • \u matches unicode characters, such as Chinese
  • \a matches only ascii characters

Practical Cases

网站链接：
https://www.example.com/page1.html?query=123&sort=desc#section2
http://sub.example.co.jp:8080/admin/dashboard
ftp://ftp.example.org/upload.zip

Extracting Phone Numbers

Explanation: first \b matches a word boundary, a group extracts the country code (2-3 digits, compatible with the + case), followed by - or a space, in lazy mode, then matches the case where 3-4 digits and - appear consecutively multiple times

Matching result:

  • +86 138-0013-8000

Capturing Product Serial Numbers (Including Date and Unique Code)

Matching result:

  • SKU-20240309-001234
  • INV-2023-Winter-Sale-0456

Matching Chinese Characters

Group extraction result: 2024-03-09T15:40:22+08:00

Extracting IP Addresses

Matching result:

  • 192.168.1.1

Conclusion

item.title: The For Command in Windows Batch Scripts
item.description:
Introduction

In our daily work, if you use Windows, making good use of batch commands, especially for bulk file and text processing, can greatly boost productivity and get twice the result with half the effort!

However, many people’s use of batch scripts stops at combining several commands to run together, saving the time of repeatedly typing commands and waiting. This is actually just the most basic way to use batch scripts.

But to unlock the full power of batch scripts, the for command is truly the core. As a tool that handles both loop processing and text-column processing, nothing rivals it when it comes to improving batch script efficiency!

Yet the for command is relatively complex to use, and many people may not have mastered it well. So in this article, we bring you a systematic introduction to this core command in batch scripting.

There’s also an Easter egg that Qiucao discovered: Microsoft actually has an official, long-standing bug that has never been fixed 😂😂😂

Introduction to the For Command

Let’s now take a detailed look at this heavyweight command in Windows batch scripting.

Basic Syntax 

1

FOR %variable IN (set) DO command [command-parameters]
  • %variable: the for-loop variable; use %% in batch scripts and % when running directly from the command line
  • (set): can be a file, a directory, a string, or command output..
  • command: the command to execute for each iteration.
  • command-parameters: control loop behavior (such as /R, /D, /L, /F, etc.)

For example, to iterate over a set:

1
2

@echo off
for %%a in (苹果 香蕉 "西瓜 芒果") do echo 水果：%%a

Output:

1
2
3

水果：苹果
水果：香蕉
水果："西瓜 芒果"
  • Note: by default, elements are separated by spaces, and a quoted string is treated as a whole.

** The /R Option: Recursively Traverse Files**

This option is used to recursively traverse files in a directory and its subdirectories.

1
2

@echo off
for /R "C:\Chengxiaqiucao" %%a in (*.txt) do echo 找到文件：%%a

Features:

  • Traverse all .txt files under C:\Chengxiaqiucao and its subdirectories.
  • %%a will contain the full file path (e.g. C:\Chengxiaqiucao\test\file.txt).

/D: Process Directories

This option traverses directories only (not files).

1
2

@echo off
for /D %%a in ("C:\*") do echo 目录：%%a

Features:

  • List all first-level directories under C:\ (such as Program Files, Users, etc.).

4. /L: Generate a Number Sequence

This option is similar to controlling the number of loop iterations when programming.

Syntax: for /L %%a in (start, step, end)

The following example generates an arithmetic sequence:

1
2

@echo off
for /L %%a in (1, 2, 10) do echo 当前数字：%%a

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

当前数字：1
当前数字：3
当前数字：5
当前数字：7
当前数字：9

/F: Advanced Text Parsing (The Core Option)

This option can be considered the most core option of the For command; in most cases, it’s what lets the For command truly shine.

It is mainly used to parse text, strings, or command output line by line, and it supports complex rules.

Syntax: 
1

for /F ["选项"] %%a in (数据源) do 命令
  • Data source: a file, a string, or command output (wrapped in backticks `).
  • Options: delims, tokens, skip, eol, usebackq, etc.

Common Options of /F

Option Purpose Example
delims=xyz Define delimiters (default space/tab) delims=, split by comma
tokens=n Extract the nth column (separate multiple columns with commas, e.g. 1,3) tokens=2 extract the second column
skip=n Skip the first n lines skip=2 skip the first two lines
eol=; Define the line comment character (default ;) eol=# ignore lines starting with #
usebackq Change how the data source is quoted (see below) Handle paths with spaces or command output

The Role of usebackq

Easter Egg Here: A Bug in the Official Documentation

In the Chinese official Windows help, the description of the -F option is actually wrong.

As you can see, the description here for using usebackq is exactly the same as for not using it, and the Chinese translation is very awkward and hard to understand.

However, by running the chcp 65001 command to switch the command-line code page to UTF-8, the help is then displayed in English.

As you can see, this is much clearer. usebackq solves the problems in the following scenarios:

  1. Handle file paths with spaces: quote the filename with double quotes.
  2. Execute a command and parse its output: quote the system command with backticks `.
  3. Parse a string directly: quote the string with single quotes '.
Case 1: 
1
2

@echo off
for /F "usebackq delims=" %%a in ("C:\My Files\data.txt") do echo %%a
  • Without usebackq, the spaces in the path would cause a parsing error.
** Case 2**

Parse data.csv (format: name,age,city), skip the header line, and extract the name and city.

Input file data.csv:

1
2
3

姓名,年龄,城市
张三,25,北京
李四,30,上海

Batch script:

1
2
3
4

@echo off
for /F "usebackq skip=1 delims=, tokens=1,3" %%a in ("data.csv") do (
 echo 姓名：%%a，城市：%%b
)

Output:

1
2

姓名：张三，城市：北京
姓名：李四，城市：上海

Application Scenario Summary

Option Applicable Scenario Typical Command Example
None Iterate over a simple list of files or strings for %%a in (*.txt) do echo %%a
/R Recursively process files under a directory for /R %%a in (*.log) do del %%a
/D Process directories only for /D %%a in (C:\*) do echo %%a
/L Generate a number sequence (e.g. a fixed number of loops) for /L %%a in (1,1,5) do echo %%a
/F Parse text files, command output, or complex strings for /F "tokens=2" %%a in (data.txt)

So by mastering these options and techniques of the For command, you can fully turn it into a “Swiss Army knife” for handling files, text, and system tasks in batch scripts.

item.title: A Guide to grep, One of the Linux Text Processing Trio
item.description:
Preface

grep is one of the Linux trio (grep, sed, awk), used to search for specific text patterns in files. It is not only powerful but also very flexible, capable of handling a wide variety of text-search needs. Below we walk through the detailed usage of the grep command and its advanced examples.

Basic Usage

Basic Search 

1

grep "pattern" filename

Used to search the filename file for lines containing pattern and print them out.

Ignoring Case 

1

grep -i "pattern" filename

Use the -i option to ignore case.

Recursive Search 

1

grep -r "pattern" directory

Recursively search the contents of files containing pattern in the directory and its subdirectories.

Showing Line Numbers 

1

grep -n "pattern" filename

Use the -n option to show the line numbers of matching lines.

Inverted Search (Show Non-Matching Lines) 

1

grep -v "pattern" filename

Use the -v option to show lines that do not contain pattern.

Showing File Names 

1

grep "pattern" file1 file2 file3

When searching multiple files, the matching file names are shown by default. Use -H to force showing file names, and use -h to hide them.

Advanced Usage

Using Regular Expressions 

1

grep -E "pattern1|pattern2" filename

Use the -E option to support extended regular expressions, where | means the OR operation.

Counting Matching Lines 

1

grep -c "pattern" filename

Use the -c option to count the number of matching lines.

Showing Only the Matched Part 

1

grep -o "pattern" filename

Use the -o option to show only the matched part instead of the entire line.

Showing Lines Before and After 

1
2
3

grep -A 3 "pattern" filename # Show the matching line and the 3 lines after it
grep -B 3 "pattern" filename # Show the matching line and the 3 lines before it
grep -C 3 "pattern" filename # Show the matching line and 3 lines before and after it

The -A, -B, and -C options are used to show a specified number of lines after, before, or both before and after the matching line, respectively.

Reading Data from Standard Input 

1

echo "some text" | grep "pattern"

grep can read data from standard input, which is very useful in pipeline operations.

Searching with Fixed Strings (Improving Performance) 

1

grep -F "fixed_string" filename

Use the -F option to treat pattern as a fixed string rather than a regular expression, which can improve search performance.

Excluding Files 

1

grep -r --exclude="*.log" "pattern" directory

Use the --exclude option to exclude files of a certain type.

Using Perl-Compatible Regular Expressions 

1

grep -P "\d+" filename

Use the -P option to enable Perl-compatible regular expressions, where \d+ means one or more digits.

Zero-Width Assertions 

1

grep -P '(?<=foo)bar' filename

Use Perl-compatible regular expressions to support zero-width assertions; for example, (?<=foo)bar matches a bar that is preceded by foo.

Combined Usage Examples

Finding Files of a Specific Type in a Specific Directory and Searching Their Contents 

1

grep -r --include="*.py" "import" /path/to/directory

Recursively search all .py files in the /path/to/directory directory for lines containing import.

Finding and Showing Matching Lines with Two Lines Before and After 

1

grep -C 2 "error" /var/log/syslog

Find lines containing error in the /var/log/syslog file and show the two lines before and after them.

Counting the Number of Files Containing a Specific Word 

1

grep -rl "word" /path/to/directory | wc -l

Recursively search the /path/to/directory directory for files containing word, and count the number of files.

Conclusion

Through these examples, you can appreciate the power and flexibility of grep, which also makes it one of the most practical text-processing tools in Linux.
